articles.title: Cardiff man thankful Calon Hearts' scan revealed 'silent' heart attack
articles.summary: A charity heart scan led to Simon Morris having surgery for a blocked artery he didn't know he had.
articles.body:
A man has described how a routine cardiac screening led to potentially life-saving treatment and showed he had unknowingly suffered a heart attack.

Simon Morris, from Cardiff, said he had no reason to believe anything was wrong when he agreed to pay £300 for a heart scan after his daughter had been offered free screening by a Welsh charity.

"I was 55, I'd never had such a scan before, so I thought, why not... just get it done and out of the way.

"It turns out it was the best £300 I've ever spent."

Morris was advised to go to hospital and tests revealed he needed an angioplasty - a procedure to reopen narrowed or blocked arteries supplying blood to the heart.

Investigations also showed he had suffered what is known as a "silent" heart attack as he had not experienced any symptoms.

But, looking back, he said there had been warning signs.

"When I was going for big walks with my daughter and my son there were pains in the chest area which I just attributed to stomach issues," he told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast .

"But now... I look back and go, 'what an idiot. You should have done something about that then. That was your chance, you missed it'."

Following cardiac rehabilitation, he has since returned to an active lifestyle, climbing Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon , aiming to raise £10,000 for charity Calon Hearts UK which provided his scan.

He said he was grateful one of its cardiologists who identified his heart problem during the scan.

And he has since been helping raise awareness of its work providing CPR training and free screening for those aged between 15 and a half and 26 and part-funded tests for those older.

"I wanted to give something back to the charity that had potentially saved my life, and if I was going to do something, it felt appropriate to take on something as big as Yr Wyddfa," said Morris.

A heart attack happens when blood flow to your heart is blocked. It can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

chest pain which may feel like crushing or squeezing on your chest - the pain may also spread to your arm, neck and jaw

feeling like you have indigestion - you may have a burning feeling in your chest and feel full or bloated

pale, blue or grey skin - on black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands

The NHS said you should call 999 if you have any symptoms.

They're often only diagnosed weeks, months or years afterwards, during a routine check-up, or because of ongoing symptoms, like chest pain or breathlessness.

Silent heart attacks are common. They are estimated to make up around a third of all heart attacks.

articles.title: Imagem de Nossa Senhora Aparecida: os detalhes do nicho blindado | G1
articles.standfirst: Imagem original fica a cerca de quatro metros do chão, no Santuário Nacional, e é protegida por uma estrutura reforçada após ter sido quebrada em mais de 200 pedaços em 1978.
articles.summary: Protegida por vidro à prova de balas, a imagem de Nossa Senhora Aparecida no Santuário Nacional guarda a história da restauração após o ataque de 1978.
articles.body:
Imagem encontrada em 1717 no Rio Paraíba do Sul fica em nicho blindado no Santuário Nacional em Aparecida — Foto: Carlos Santos/g1

Com cerca de 500 quilos, o vidro à prova de balas que protege a imagem original de Nossa Senhora Aparecida é uma das barreiras de segurança que cercam a escultura no Santuário Nacional, em Aparecida (SP). A imagem fica a aproximadamente quatro metros do chão, em um nicho que permite a contemplação dos devotos e ajuda a preservar a peça histórica.

A proteção ganhou relevância diante de um dos episódios mais marcantes da história da escultura. Em 16 de maio de 1978, durante uma missa na Basílica Histórica de Aparecida, um jovem aproveitou um apagão para furtar a imagem de um cofre e a jogou no chão. O impacto fez com que a peça se partisse em mais de 200 pedaços.

Após o episódio, a imagem foi levada ao Museu de Arte de São Paulo (Masp), onde a restauradora Maria Helena Chartuni ficou responsável pela reconstrução. Na época, ela não era devota de Nossa Senhora Aparecida e inicialmente encarou o serviço como mais um trabalho. Ao ver a extensão dos danos, principalmente na cabeça da escultura, ficou impressionada com o desafio.

Chartuni trabalhou durante 33 dias para recompor a imagem, utilizando cola de secagem rápida e reconstruindo as partes danificadas. Durante o processo, rezou e pediu ajuda a Nossa Senhora. A restauradora contou que a experiência transformou sua relação com a fé e fez com que se tornasse devota da santa.

Em 19 de agosto de 1978, a imagem restaurada voltou a Aparecida em um caminhão do Corpo de Bombeiros, acompanhada por uma multidão de fiéis. A chegada foi marcada por orações e demonstrações de emoção de pessoas que se reuniram para receber a escultura de volta.

Atualmente, a imagem original permanece exposta no Santuário Nacional, em um nicho elevado e protegido. A estrutura permite que os visitantes contemplem a escultura sem contato direto com a peça histórica.

O nicho também reúne elementos decorativos com significado religioso. O revestimento conta com pastilhas de porcelana pintadas a ouro, enquanto a decoração inclui peixes em alto-relevo, em referência à pesca milagrosa, e um sol associado à passagem bíblica da “mulher vestida de sol”.

Ondas representam o Espírito Santo, e círculos remetem à perfeição divina. A estrutura também traz a inscrição: “O Espírito e a Esposa dizem: Amém. Vem Senhor Jesus”, trecho do livro do Apocalipse.

articles.title: VÍDEO: rio transborda, alaga propriedade rural e arrasta bezerros após chuva intensa no Paraná | G1
articles.standfirst: Alagamento aconteceu em Capitão Leônidas Marques, no oeste do estado. Município registrou 150 milímetros de chuva em 48 horas. Produtor relata perda de até dez bezerros e prejuízos em lavouras.
articles.summary: Alagamento aconteceu em Capitão Leônidas Marques, no oeste do estado. Município registrou 150 milímetros de chuva em 48 horas. Produtor relata perda de até dez bezerros e prejuízos
articles.body:
O Rio Monteiro transbordou, alagou uma propriedade rural e arrastou bezerros que estavam confinados em uma fazenda de gabo em Capitão Leônidas Marques , no oeste do Paraná, neste sábado (10). O produtor rural Dilamar Quadri contou que precisou da ajuda de outras pessoas para retirar os animais do local. Veja as imagens acima.

"Morrendo ovelha, porco, bezerro... Perdemos alguns bezerros. Isso é coisa de outro mundo [...] Água levou embora a bicharada", lamentou o produtor.

Segundo o Centro Nacional de Monitoramento e Alertas de Desastres Naturais (Cemaden), o município registrou 150 milímetros de chuva entre sábado e domingo (11).

Na propriedade de Dilamar, cerca de 1,1 mil cabeças de gado são mantidas em uma área de confinamento que foi invadida pela água do rio.

Pelo menos oito animais foram arrastados durante o alagamento — Foto: Rui Castro

O produtor relatou que perdeu entre oito e dez bezerros, que foram levados pela correnteza. O número exato de animais perdidos ainda não foi confirmado.

Em entrevista à RPC , afiliada da TV Globo , Dilamar contou que somente depois que a chuva diminuiu foi possível avaliar parte dos prejuízos.

articles.title: Vacinação antirrábica em Angra dos Reis começa nesta terça | G1
articles.standfirst: Imunização gratuita de cães e gatos será realizada até sexta-feira (16), das 9h às 13h, em bairros de quatro distritos do município.
articles.summary: Imunização gratuita de cães e gatos será realizada até sexta-feira (16), das 9h às 13h, em bairros de quatro distritos do município.
articles.body:
Vacinação antirrábica em Angra dos Reis começa nesta terça; confira os locais. — Foto: Divulgação/Prefeitura de Angra dos Reis

A segunda semana da campanha de vacinação antirrábica em Angra dos Reis (RJ) começa nesta terça-feira (13) e segue até sexta-feira (16). A imunização gratuita de cães e gatos será realizada das 9h às 13h, em diferentes pontos do município.

A campanha é promovida pela Secretaria Municipal de Saúde. Neste ano, a meta é vacinar 20 mil animais em toda a cidade.

Segundo a prefeitura, devem receber a vacina cães e gatos saudáveis a partir de três meses de idade. A imunização é importante para prevenir a raiva, doença grave que pode ser transmitida aos seres humanos.

Os cães devem ser levados com coleira e guia, conduzidos por adultos capazes de contê-los. Já os gatos precisam ser transportados em caixas apropriadas para evitar fugas e acidentes.

A vacina é aplicada pelas equipes responsáveis nos pontos da campanha. As doses não podem ser retiradas pelos tutores para aplicação em casa.

Vila Velha: próximo ao salão comunitário;

Tanguá e Praia Grande: vacinação volante;;

Boa Vista: quadra do Morro da Boa Vista;

Santa Rita II: praça do campo de futebol

Banqueta: ESF Vale da Banqueta e ESF Banqueta I

Camorim Grande: vacinação volante no morro

Camorim Pequeno: Associação de Moradores

articles.title: Explosão mata jovem de 15 anos e deixa 19 feridos no norte de Israel | G1
articles.standfirst: Ônibus com adolescentes e professores foi atingido por munição não detonada durante passeio escolar. Autoridades do governo Netanyahu lamentaram nas redes sociais.
articles.summary: Ônibus com adolescentes e professores foi atingido por munição não detonada durante passeio escolar. Autoridades do governo Netanyahu lamentaram nas redes sociais.
articles.body:
Cena de uma explosão na área de Ramim Ridge, no norte de Israel, perto da fronteira com o Líbano, provavelmente resultado de um artefato explosivo não detonado, em 12 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Magen David Adom

Um jovem morreu nesta segunda-feira (12) em uma explosão que deixou cerca de 19 feridos, muitos deles adolescentes, durante um passeio escolar no norte de Israel, perto da fronteira com o Líbano.

O grupo, formado por alunos e professores de uma escola religiosa, estava em uma viagem perto de Neot Mordechai quando foi atingido pela explosão de uma munição não detonada que estava no trajeto, de acordo com um comunicado da polícia.

A notícia foi confirmada na rede social X por Israel Katz, ministro da Defesa de Israel, que lamentou o incidente:

"Compartilho a profunda dor da família do jovem que perdeu a vida na explosão ocorrida durante a excursão perto da fronteira norte, e desejo uma recuperação pronta e completa a todos os feridos".

O tipo de munição que explodiu e sua procedência ainda não foram revelados pelas autoridades.

Gideon Sa'ar, ministro das Relações Exteriores de Israel, também se pronunciou sobre a tragédia no X e revelou que a vítima fatal foi um menino de 15 anos:

"Meu coração está em luto pela terrível tragédia na fronteira norte. Um menino de 15 anos, que fazia sua viagem anual, não voltará para casa. Compartilho da dor e do profundo pesar da família e da Yeshiva da Escola Secundária Ort Maalot. Desejo uma recuperação completa e rápida aos feridos".

Após o anúncio da explosão, o Magen David Adom (MDA), equivalente israelense da Cruz Vermelha, declarou que suas equipes estavam atendendo no local "oito feridos em estado grave ou moderado, assim como vários outros com ferimentos leves".

As Forças de Defesa de Israel deslocaram militares e helicópteros da Força Aérea para auxiliar no resgate das vítimas.

O Exército israelense afirmou que as circunstâncias da explosão estão sendo investigadas.

articles.title: Ataque a tiros em escola na França deixa feridos | G1
articles.standfirst: Adolescente de 14 anos atirou contra funcionários com espingarda, segundo governo francês. Suspeito foi detido pela polícia. Ataque a tiros ocorreu em meio a semanas de protestos estudantis por todo o país europeu, que causaram crise política e social.
articles.summary: Adolescente de 14 anos atirou contra funcionários com espingarda, segundo governo francês. Suspeito foi detido pela polícia. Ataque a tiros ocorreu em meio a semanas de protestos estudantis por todo o país europeu, que causaram crise política e social.
articles.body:
Um ataque a tiros em uma escola na França nesta segunda-feira (12) deixou dois feridos, segundo o governo francês. Um aluno de 14 anos foi preso sob suspeita de levar uma espingarda e disparar contra funcionários.

O incidente ocorreu na escola Lakanal em Aubagne, cidade no extremo sul do país próxima a Marselha. O diretor do colégio e uma professora ficaram feridos após serem atingidos por disparos de uma espingarda de caça , segundo o gabinete do primeiro-ministro francês, Sébastien Lecornu.

O autor do ataque é um aluno de 14 anos, segundo o prefeito Jean-Pierre Squillari. Ele levou a espingarda escondida dentro de uma capa de guitarra e abriu fogo quando chegou à escola. O adolescente foi desarmado por um supervisor e foi detido pela polícia, segundo o relato do prefeito e de um colega da escola.

Alunos e pais do lado de fora da escola Lakanal em Aubagne, no extremo sul da França, após ataque a tiros em 12 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reuters

O diretor e a professora foram internados e atendimento médico no local e nenhum dos dois corre risco de morrer , afirmou o gabinete do premiê.

Squillari disse que seu governo abriu uma investigação para apurar o ataque.

Viaturas de polícia e ambulâncias do lado de fora da escola Lakanal em Aubagne, no extremo sul da França, após ataque a tiros em 12 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reuters

Uma estudante do nono ano da escola Lakanal disse à agência de notícias Reuters que os alunos saíram correndo das salas de aula quando ouviram os dois disparos de espingarda.

“Ouvimos estrondos e saímos da sala. Pareciam fogos de artifício estourando, mas depois percebemos que eram tiros. Eu e meu amigo olhamos para trás e ele [aluno autor do ataque] estava lá carregando uma arma. Então, entramos em pânico e corremos. (...) Havia sangue nos dois primeiros andares. Não sabíamos o que estava acontecendo. O instinto de sobrevivência falou mais alto, e corri em direção à saída. (...) Fiquei assustada, eu poderia ter morrido”, disse a estudante.

Segundo a aluna, que não teve sua identidade revelada, sua professora de matemática inicialmente havia minimizado o barulho causado pelo primeiro disparo, atribuindo-o a obras nas proximidades. Porém, o segundo disparo foi seguido pelo acionamento de um alarme.

O ataque ocorreu em meio a protestos estudantis que tomaram as ruas da França nas últimas semanas. O movimento causou um caos no país europeu e gerou uma crise política , com combates entre manifestantes e policiais, centenas de escolas fechadas e aulas suspensas, além de uma greve de professores.

Eddy Sid, porta-voz do sindicato policial SGP-FO, disse à BFM TV que não havia nenhuma ligação aparente entre o ataque e os protestos de estudantes do Ensino Médio contra a falta de funcionários e de financiamento para as escolas. Segundo Sid, o colégio Lakanal não havia sido afetado pelos protestos.

O presidente francês, Emmanuel Macron, que tenta estancar a crise causada pelos protestos estudantis, lamentou o ataque desta segunda. Ele afirmou também que a violência nas manifestações protestos estudantis é "inaceitável".

A líder da extrema direita, Marine Le Pen, favorita na disputa para substituir Macron na próxima primavera europeia, afirmou que o governo estava perdendo o controle da segurança nas escolas.

“As escolas, que deveriam ser locais de proteção, agora são lugares onde as pessoas correm risco de vida. A insegurança entrou nas escolas. Muitos alunos e professores vão para lá com um nó no estômago.”

Os ministros do Interior francês, Laurent Nuñez, e da Educação, Edouard Geffray, foram enviados à cidade após o ataque, ainda segundo o gabinete de Lecornu.

articles.title: Radares em Ribeirão Preto começam a operar na terça; veja locais | G1
articles.standfirst: Fiscalização eletrônica contará com 27 equipamentos ativados progressivamente em avenidas da cidade. Transição ocorre após o fim dos radares móveis.
articles.summary: A fiscalização eletrônica com radares em Ribeirão Preto será retomada gradualmente em 27 locais para substituir os antigos modelos móveis nas avenidas.
articles.body:
Radar fixo instalado na Avenida Marechal Costa e Silva, em Ribeirão Preto (SP). — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

A Prefeitura de Ribeirão Preto (SP) dará início à operação gradual dos radares fixos nas avenidas a partir de terça-feira (13) . Nesta primeira etapa , serão ativados equipamentos de fiscalização eletrônica nos seguintes trechos:

Avenida Saudade x Avenida Francisco Junqueira

Rua Sergipe x Avenida Francisco Junqueira

Avenida Fábio Barreto x Avenida Jerônimo Gonçalves

Avenida Costábile Romano (em frente o Parque Curupira)

A ativação dos demais pontos -- são 27 no total (veja abaixo os endereços) -- ocorrerá ao longo da semana, de acordo com as condições técnicas e de sinalização de cada ponto.

De acordo com a administração municipal, a prioridade é garantir que todos os trechos estejam sinalizados com placas de limite de velocidade antes do início da fiscalização e da aplicação de multas.

Segundo a Prefeitura, a mudança busca adotar uma fiscalização mais previsível e transparente, com radares em locais permanentes e visíveis aos condutores, visando incentivar o respeito às regras e prevenir acidentes.

Os pontos de instalação foram definidos com base em estudos de engenharia de tráfego que avaliaram fatores como fluxo de veículos e histórico de acidentes. A operação do sistema é da RP Mobi, empresa que gerencia o trânsito na cidade, por meio do Consórcio Vias Inteligentes.

Os 27 equipamentos desta fase inicial estão distribuídos em trechos e cruzamentos das seguintes vias:

Avenida Eduardo Andrea Matarazzo (Via Norte)

Avenida Carlos Eduardo de Gasperi Consoni

Avenida Dr. Francisco Junqueira com a Avenida Saudade

Avenida Dr. Francisco Junqueira com a Rua Sergipe

Avenida Fábio Barreto com a Avenida Jerônimo Gonçalves

Avenida Deputado Sérgio Cardoso de Almeida

O novo sistema tem 18 radares fixos de velocidade, cinco equipamentos híbridos, que monitoram tanto o excesso de velocidade quanto o avanço do sinal vermelho, e quatro lombadas eletrônicas, que exibem em painéis a velocidade para alertar motoristas.

Os novos equipamentos contam ainda com a tecnologia de leitura automática de placas, capaz de identificar veículos que trafegam indevidamente por faixas exclusivas de ônibus.

Radar fixo em testes na Avenida Marechal Costa e Silva, em Ribeirão Preto (SP). — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

A reestruturação na fiscalização eletrônica começou em dezembro de 2025, quando a Prefeitura anunciou o fim dos radares móveis operados por agentes de trânsito.

A substituição veio com a justificativa de que a fiscalização deve ser educativa, em vez de gerar a sensação de punição injusta e que existe uma "indústria da multa" na cidade.

A administração municipal também justificou a implantação dos pontos permanentes com base nos índices de violência no trânsito.

A empresa responsável foi contratada por meio de licitação na modalidade pregão presencial, vencida pelo Consórcio RP Vias Inteligentes. O valor estimado da contratação foi mantido sob sigilo.

Durante o período em que os radares móveis deixaram de operar, Ribeirão Preto teve um recuo no volume de autuações de trânsito.

Agente de trânsito da RP Mobi opera radar móvel em Ribeirão Preto, SP — Foto: Acervo EP

articles.title: Nonagenários renovam votos após mais de 70 anos de casamento: 'Parece que foram 7 dias' | G1
articles.standfirst: Relacionamento começou como amizade na década de 1950, em Minas Gerais. Agora Joaquim Bárbara Moreira, de 95 anos, e Antonieta Silva Moreira, de 93 anos, compartilham os dias juntos em Curitiba.
articles.summary: Relacionamento começou como amizade nos anos 50, em Minas Gerais. Agora Joaquim Moreira, de 95 anos, e Antonieta Silva Moreira, de 93 anos, compartilham os dias juntos em Curitiba.
articles.body:
Mesmo com mais de 70 anos de casamento, Joaquim Bárbara Moreira e Antonieta Silva Moreira se recusam a deixar o romantismo de lado e renovaram os votos.

Joaquim, de 95 anos, e Antonieta, de 93 anos, celebraram as décadas juntos neste sábado (10), em Curitiba .

A união dos dois rendeu três filhos, sete netos e uma bisneta, que se juntam a cerca de 80 convidados para comemorar as "bodas de vinho" do casal.

"Eu não tenho nem muitas palavras para falar, porque a gente viveu bem para caramba. Se eu pudesse voltar para começar tudo de novo e fazer igual, eu voltaria. Eu vivi 70 anos [com Antonieta], parece que foram 7 dias", afirma Joaquim.

O relacionamento começou como uma amizade na década de 1950, no interior de Minas Gerais, quando os dois eram bem jovens.

Joaquim Bárbara Moreira e Antonieta Silva Moreira — Foto: Paulo Kreling/RPC

"Nós brincávamos muito. Eu e ele já nos conhecíamos e nos tratávamos de comadre e compadre. Ele foi o primeiro e o último [namorado]", lembra Antonina.

O segredo para a longevidade do relacionamento, segundo o casal, é o respeito e o amor.

"É amor, né. Eu cuido dele e ele cuida de mim", conta Antonina.

"Ela me respeitou muito bem e eu respeitei ela também", diz Joaquim.

A comemoração contou com tudo aquilo que o casal mais gosta, inclusive a empolgação: Joaquim exigiu três barris de chope para que os convidados aproveitem a festa.

"Essa festa vai ser muito legal, a gente preparou com muito carinho. A gente fez do jeitinho que ele queria, porque ele quer churrasco e chope. Então vai ser assim, da forma como ele quer. Ele fez questão do chope. Ele não bebe, mas sabe que nós gostamos", explica a filha do casal, Ester Moreira.

Casal está junto há 70 anos — Foto: Paulo Kreling/RPC

articles.title: SC restored people's faith: Kapil Sibal a day after venting frustration
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court's order Sunday finding prima facie breach of its Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of Metro and train services and issuing
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court's order Sunday finding prima facie breach of its Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of Metro and train services and issuing notice to Union home secretary, Delhi Police commissioner and Delhi Metro chief altered over the course of a day senior advocate and Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal's views on the apex court.On Saturday, Sibal had told reporters "if we go to courts, I do not know whether we will ever get relief. The people of this country have decided that this govt has to go. If anyone can save the Constitution at this juncture, it is Supreme Court."He added, "I am tired of repeatedly approaching the SC. It's in my mind that there is no purpose in going there. I have not much expectations from SC. Whatever is to happen will happen. I only pray the country's democracy remains intact... The tribunals (in West Bengal) have allowed appeals of 93% voters whose names were deleted illegally. SC has come to know this. But we did not get any relief".On Sunday, he was leading a 100-strong team of lawyers in SC to question the detentions of protesters and alleged violations of court's Oct 9 order against shutdown of Metro and rail services. The emotionally charged arguments saw pro-protester lawyers paint a picture of injustice and violation of fundamental rights on Saturday, compare it to an "undeclared emergency" and shout down a senior advocate who said lawyers must confine their activities to courts and not hit the streets, and that freedom of speech came with reasonable restrictions.At an appropriate juncture, Justice Joymalya Bagchi said, "Our purpose is to instil people's faith in the system, and in that process your (lawyer's) confidence is most vital for our fight against injustice." The court also passed a slew of directives, including normalising Metro, train and internet services and traffic in the city and allowing lawyers and journalists to carry out professional work.Soon after the SC order, Sibal said, "We are deeply grateful to the Supreme Court for passing an order that restores the faith of the Indian people, as well as the faith of professionals, in the justice system of this country."Within an hour of SC passing the order, a senior advocate entered into an argument with cops over removal of barricades, citing the SC ruling. articles.title: 12 Australian farming families were fined $814 each for blocking surveyors; they say a proposed 480-kilometre power line threatens their land
articles.summary: Twelve farming families in western Victoria, Australia, have been fined A$814 each for refusing to allow authorised officers onto their properties to
articles.body: Twelve farming families in western Victoria, Australia, have been fined A$814 each for refusing to allow authorised officers onto their properties to conduct surveys for a proposed 480-kilometre electricity transmission line. The families say the project, known as Victoria to New South Wales Interconnector West (VNI West), threatens agricultural land, farm operations and the future of properties that some have worked for generations. Another six landowners received formal warnings after denying access. The fines, issued in August 2026, have intensified opposition to the multibillion-dollar infrastructure project, with affected farmers challenging the government's approach to private property access. The dispute has since moved towards a legal challenge, while the project's environmental assessment remains underway.Why were 12 Australian farming families fined?The Victorian government issued the infringement notices on August 4, 2026, after the landholders refused access to authorised officers seeking to undertake preliminary investigations for VNI West. The notices alleged that the farmers had hindered, obstructed or delayed authorised activities without a reasonable excuse. The fines were issued under Victoria's Electricity Industry Act 2000, which provides powers for authorised officers to access land for specified electricity infrastructure planning activities. Six other property owners received formal warnings for refusing access.The farmers argue that their refusal was linked to concerns about the timing of inspections, agricultural activities and the potential consequences of the proposed transmission line. They maintain that they should have greater control over access to their properties, particularly when visits could interfere with livestock management or other time-sensitive farming work.What is the proposed 480-kilometre power line?VNI West is a proposed high-voltage transmission project designed to strengthen electricity connections between Victoria and New South Wales. It would connect renewable energy zones and electricity networks across the two states, helping transport power between generation sources and major demand centres. The Victorian section involves a proposed 500-kilovolt, double-circuit overhead transmission line running from the Bulgana area in western Victoria towards a terminal station at Tragowel, before continuing north towards the Murray River near Kerang. From there, the project would connect with infrastructure in New South Wales.The project is intended to improve electricity reliability, support the integration of renewable energy and provide access to generation and storage resources across state borders. Its estimated cost has been reported in the range of A7.6billiontoA11.4 billion for the wider project. However, the proposed route crosses agricultural regions where farming is a major economic activity. Landholders along the alignment have raised concerns about the placement of transmission towers, access tracks and easements, as well as the potential effects on land use and property values.Farmers fear damage to their land and livelihoodsFor the affected families, the dispute is not simply about surveyors entering their properties. They are concerned about what the eventual infrastructure could mean for their farms, businesses and the land they hope to pass on to future generations. Trent Carter, a fifth-generation sheep farmer from Wallaloo East in western Victoria, objected to surveyors entering a paddock during lambing season. He said the visit could put his stud Merino sheep at risk and argued that the authorities had not adequately considered animal welfare and the timing of agricultural operations.Carter said his family had attempted to negotiate a more suitable inspection time but felt their concerns were not properly addressed. He subsequently said he intended to contest the fine rather than pay it. Other landholders have raised concerns about the effect of transmission infrastructure on farm layouts, bushfire preparedness and the marketability of their properties. They fear that the presence of large towers and associated infrastructure could complicate agricultural operations and reduce the appeal of their land to prospective buyers.A 103-year-old farm and concerns about protected wildlifeColin and Mary Fenton, an elderly farming couple from the Kerang area, were among the landholders reported to have received fines. Their family has farmed the property for more than a century. Colin Fenton said the couple had raised concerns about a protected wedge-tailed eagle nest on their property. He questioned whether their objections had been adequately considered before the access notices were enforced.The couple also expressed concerns about the effect of the proposed project on their farm's value. Fenton said he had approached a real estate agent about selling the property but feared that the planned transmission infrastructure could make it harder to find a buyer. Their concerns highlight the broader questions surrounding the project's environmental assessment, including how wildlife habitats, agricultural land and existing land uses will be considered when the final route and associated infrastructure are determined.Farmers refuse to pay and prepare a legal challengeThe fines have prompted affected landholders to coordinate their response. Regional reporting in August indicated that the farmers intended to obtain legal representation and challenge the notices. By October 6, the Herald Sun reported that all 12 families had refused to pay and had secured an extension until October 23 after seeking an appeal through joint legal representation.The dispute centres partly on whether the farmers had a reasonable excuse for denying access and whether the enforcement measures were appropriate in the circumstances. The authorities maintain that authorised officers have legal powers to conduct specified planning activities and that landholders were notified of proposed visits. The legal challenge could bring greater scrutiny to how these powers are exercised when survey work affects active farms, including the consideration given to seasonal work, livestock welfare and biosecurity.The fines do not themselves determine whether the transmission project will ultimately be approved. They concern access for planning and survey activities, while the project's environmental and planning approvals follow a separate process.Government says survey access is necessary for planningVicGrid, the Victorian government body responsible for planning the state's transmission network, has argued that surveys are needed to understand the land and environmental conditions along the proposed route. Such investigations can examine biodiversity, waterways, cultural heritage, agriculture and other factors that may influence the project's design and potential impacts. The information is intended to inform the environmental assessment and identify measures to avoid or reduce harm.Authorities have said they sought voluntary access agreements with landholders before using statutory powers. The government has also pointed to notice periods and other engagement measures as part of its approach. The farmers, however, argue that notification alone does not adequately address their concerns when proposed visits conflict with critical farming activities. The disagreement has therefore become a test of how infrastructure planners balance statutory access rights with the practical realities of running agricultural businesses.Environmental assessment remains underwayThe Victorian component of VNI West is undergoing an environmental effects statement (EES), a detailed assessment of the project's potential environmental, social and economic consequences. The Victorian planning department says the EES was required in April 2024. It is intended to examine issues including biodiversity, native vegetation, cultural heritage, waterways, agriculture, land use and effects on communities.The EES went on public exhibition on October 5, 2026, with submissions open until November 16. An Inquiry and Advisory Committee directions hearing is scheduled for December 7, followed by a main hearing expected to begin in the week of February 8, 2027. The process will allow the project's evidence and public submissions to be considered before the planning minister makes the relevant assessment. The route and project design remain subject to the applicable assessment and approval requirements.For the farmers opposing the scheme, the assessment is a critical opportunity to have concerns about their land and livelihoods examined. For the project proponents, the process is intended to establish the likely effects of the infrastructure and determine how those effects can be managed.VNI West becomes a political issue in VictoriaOpposition to the transmission line has also become a point of political contention ahead of Victoria's November 2026 state election. In August, the Liberal and National parties pledged to scrap VNI West if the Coalition won the election, arguing that the project was not viable and that alternatives should be explored. The Victorian government defended the project, saying new transmission infrastructure would be important for electricity reliability as ageing coal-fired power stations retire. The debate reflects competing views about the future of Victoria's energy system. Supporters of VNI West say stronger interconnections are needed to transport renewable electricity and maintain reliable supply. Opponents question the project's cost, its effects on rural communities and whether alternative energy investments could achieve similar objectives.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft':  As IAF trains with F-35 fighters, US guards secrets
articles.summary: The US Air Force has been protective of the F-35 at the second edition of Exercise Tarang Shakti.
articles.body: The US Air Force has been protective of the F-35 at the second edition of Exercise Tarang Shakti. This was the first time that the advanced fifth-generation fighter has flown in India airspace in an operational manner. The F-35 has made appearances at the Aero India, a biennial aerospace and defence exhibition held at Yelahanka in Bengaluru. Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, while seated next to General Kevin Schneider, Commander of the US Pacific Air Forces, during a press conference in Jodhpur stated “Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft, and you talk about selling it to us.” The IAF Chief also said, in response to another question that “The US did not show us the cockpit, but allowed us to fly in close formation.”General Schneider did clarify that the decision was not his to make. Programme-level security classification guides, he said, determine what can be shared, when it is shared and how it is protected.The importance of fifth-generation fightersFifth generation aircraft are built to reduce their radar cross-section through advanced composite airframes, careful shaping, internal weapons bays and radar-absorbent materials, which helps them survive in contested airspace. They also fuse data from the AESA radar, distributed aperture system, electronic warfare suite and infrared search-and-track sensors into a single real-time picture for the pilot. Designed to work in a network, they continuously receive information from airborne early warning aircraft, satellites, ground sensors and other fighters, giving pilots situational awareness that has changed how air combat is fought, giving the air crew an edge.India's own route to such a jet is the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft. Earlier this month, the Chief called for the programme to be accelerated, warning that further delays could force the service to look at alternative fifth-generation fighters. He said Russia had offered the Su-57, but no decision had been taken on it. He also voiced concern over Pakistan's reported efforts to acquire fifth-generation fighters with Chinese assistance, while maintaining that India has the capability to counter such threats through an integrated military system. At the same time the air force chief has described unmanned aerial systems as evolutionary rather than revolutionary for the IAF, which has operated them for decades. The force is expanding their number and types, he said, and loitering munitions have helped disrupt enemy air-defence assets.The air force has also flagged delays in Tejas Mk-1A deliveries, which are weighing on the IAF's declining fighter strength. The force is counting on the Tejas Mk-1A, the underdevelopment Tejas Mk-2 and additional 114 Rafale aircraft to bridge its capability gaps. On Sunday, the Chief flew a Tejas fighter from the Jodhpur airbase, his last flight before he retires on October 31. The IAF currently operates initial and final operational clearance configurations as it awaits the Tejas Mk-1A.

articles.title: A Michigan couple bought land at a 2015 tax sale and claimed a 50-foot strip lost through a 1965 deed error; after two surveys put it with their neighbour, an appeals court ruled against them
articles.summary: A couple in Michigan, United States, has lost a legal battle over a 50-foot-wide strip of land that they claimed belonged to their property because of an
articles.body: A couple in Michigan, United States, has lost a legal battle over a 50-foot-wide strip of land that they claimed belonged to their property because of an error in a deed dating back to 1965. Max W. Firman III and Dawn M. Kasner, who purchased their land at a tax sale in 2015, argued that the disputed strip had been used by previous owners of their property for decades. However, the Michigan Court of Appeals ruled against them on Friday, finding that they had not provided enough evidence to establish ownership.According to court documents, the dispute involved neighbouring properties in Rose Township, Ogemaw County. Firman and Kasner bought their parcel in 2015, while their neighbour, Antonio Santos, purchased the surrounding property in 2021. The disagreement began when Santos challenged the couple's claim over the strip of land, which also contained a structure.The couple believed that a mistake made in a 1965 tax sale deed had changed the description of their property's boundary. They relied on an earlier deed from 1955, which referred to a boundary measurement of 400 feet. However, the 1965 deed used 450 feet, and that description continued to appear in subsequent property records.The difference of 50 feet became the centre of the dispute. Although the couple claimed that the land and the structure on it had been used by previous owners of their property, two surveys commissioned by Santos placed the disputed area within his property. The disagreement eventually reached the courts, where the couple sought legal recognition of their ownership.How a 1965 deed became the centre of the disputeThe couple argued that the change in the property description in 1965 was an error that had remained uncorrected for decades. They maintained that the disputed strip should have been included with the land they purchased in 2015.They also claimed that previous owners had built, maintained and used the structure located on the disputed land. According to their case, they continued using the area after purchasing the property and believed that taxes had been paid on it by them and earlier owners.Santos disputed these claims. After buying the surrounding property in 2021, he commissioned two surveys, both of which showed that the 50-foot strip belonged to his property.He also submitted a photograph of the structure taken before the 2015 tax sale. A sign on the building read "NOT IN TAX SALE". Santos said his immediate predecessor had placed the sign there because photographs used in the tax sale listing had created the impression that the disputed area was included in the property being sold.Disagreement escalated after locks were changedThe dispute became more serious after Santos purchased his property. Both sides accused each other of entering the disputed area without permission.In 2023, the local sheriff was contacted after Santos allegedly changed the locks on the structure and demolished some interior walls. The sheriff told the couple that the ownership dispute would have to be settled in court.Firman and Kasner filed a lawsuit in February 2024, seeking to establish ownership of the disputed land and raising a trespass claim. Santos responded with counterclaims, including trespass and nuisance.The trial court subsequently ruled in Santos's favour, finding that the couple's original claim was barred by Michigan's 15-year limitation period. The couple then amended their complaint, arguing that they and previous owners had acquired ownership through adverse possession or acquiescence.What evidence did the couple present?To support their case, the couple submitted a 1982 deed and a 2013 affidavit concerning earlier owners of their property.The 1982 deed referred to land possessed by the previous owners for more than 15 years "in this vicinity". The couple argued that this showed the earlier owners had already acquired rights over the disputed area.The 2013 affidavit also referred to an adverse possession claim by a previous owner, Vianne Samuels, concerning property interests not clearly established in the recorded ownership documents.Adverse possession is a legal principle under which someone may acquire ownership of land through possession that meets specific legal requirements over a prescribed period. In Michigan, the relevant period is 15 years.However, the appeals court found that neither document identified the disputed 50-foot strip. Both also continued to use the same property description found in the 1965 deed.The couple relied on tax records and the existence of the structure as further evidence. But the court found that these records did not establish who had built or used the structure, when it was built, or whether the disputed land had been openly and continuously possessed for the required period.Michigan appeals court ruled against the coupleThe appeals court also considered the couple's argument of acquiescence, under which neighbouring owners may establish a property boundary by treating it as the accepted boundary for 15 years.The judges found insufficient evidence that previous owners of the neighbouring properties had accepted the boundary claimed by the couple. The sign stating "NOT IN TAX SALE" also indicated that Santos's immediate predecessor had not accepted their claimed boundary.In its October 9 ruling, the Michigan Court of Appeals upheld the trial court's decision dismissing the couple's amended complaint.However, the case has not ended entirely. The appeals court sent it back to the trial court for further proceedings concerning Santos's outstanding counterclaims, which were not decided in the appeal.You use AI every day. articles.summary: MUMBAI: The familiar red BEST bus once left Borivli station (East) before dawn, carrying vegetable and fruit vendors to Vashi's APMC market.
articles.body: MUMBAI: The familiar red BEST bus once left Borivli station (East) before dawn, carrying vegetable and fruit vendors to Vashi's APMC market. Later, office-goers, IT professionals and private-sector employees used it to travel from Navi Mumbai towards Powai, SEEPZ, Andheri and Goregaon. After years of curtailment, BEST discontinued Route A471, formerly 524L, this month.Bus enthusiast and commuter Shubham Padave, campaigning for its revival for four years, has proposed four to five morning and evening peak-hour trips via the Eastern Express Highway, using newly inducted blade-battery electric buses with greater range. The route's decline began in July 2021, when most trips were curtailed to Ghatkopar depot. By September, buses no longer reached Vashi. In September 2024, the Borivli-Ghatkopar service became air-conditioned and was renamed A471.Passenger frequency fell until only one trip remained. BEST officials cited "low passenger response" for the cancellation. A senior official said curtailed or cancelled routes could be reviewed once more buses became available.Regular commuters Harish Kulkarni and Meeta Salvi also urged BEST to restart the route with a few peak-hour trips, expanding the service when buses become available. Priti Mhatre, a Goregaon commuter, said its loss meant losing a direct, affordable connection that saved time and multiple transfers.BEST said commuters could use parallel routes 489 Ltd and A-470, or A-458 and A-460 from Gandhi Nagar.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Two Indian seafarers are missing after a tanker carrying 11 Indian crew members came under a drone attack at Sohar Anchorage in Oman on Sunday,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Two Indian seafarers are missing after a tanker carrying 11 Indian crew members came under a drone attack at Sohar Anchorage in Oman on Sunday, Union minister for ports, shipping and waterways Sarbananda Sonowal said. Nine crew members have been rescued and are safe, while search-and-rescue operations are underway.Sonowal said the tanker, MT Petro Dolphin, was attacked on October 11 and that Indian authorities were coordinating with local agencies to locate the missing seafarers."On Oct 11, tanker MT PETRO DOLPHIN, carrying 11 Indian seafarers, was subjected to a drone attack at Sohar Anchorage.While nine of our Indian crew members have been successfully rescued and are safe, two Indian nationals currently remain missing. Search-and-rescue operations are actively underway by the local Coast Guard.We are continuously coordinating with all relevant authorities to fully support the ongoing rescue efforts and ensure every possible action is taken to safely locate our missing personnel," Sonowal said in a post on X.The Embassy of India in Muscat said it was closely monitoring the situation involving the Nicaragua-flagged tanker and maintaining contact with the concerned authorities."The Embassy is closely monitoring the situation concerning MT Petro Dolphin, a Nicaragua-flagged tanker. Two of the 11 Indian seafarers onboard are reported missing. The Embassy is in close and continuous contact with the concerned authorities," the embassy said on X.The incident comes days after another commercial vessel carrying Indian crew members was attacked off Oman.On October 6, India condemned the attack on the Panama-flagged vessel MT On Peace, which was struck by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The vessel had 19 crew members, including 17 Indian nationals. According to the ministry of external affairs (MEA), 12 crew members, including 11 Indians, were injured."We condemn the attack earlier today on a Panama-flagged commercial vessel MT On Peace (IMO 9893204) off the coast of Oman, where it was struck by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. articles.title: Suspect in deadly Philadelphia police ambush faces 76 charges, ordered held without bail
articles.summary: A Philadelphia man faces 76 charges, including murder, after allegedly ambushing police officers, killing one and wounding another, according to officials.
articles.body: The suspect accused in the ambush killing of a Philadelphia police officer was arraigned Sunday morning on 76 charges and ordered held without bail, according to court records. Eric Lewis, 35, faces charges including murder, homicide of a law enforcement officer, attempted murder, 10 counts of attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer, aggravated assault, terroristic threats and other related offenses. His next court date is scheduled for Oct. 26. The charges stem from a Saturday shooting that killed Philadelphia Police Officer Shane Seiber and left his partner wounded. Seiber, 40, was a father of two and an Air Force veteran who served 10 years with the Philadelphia Police Department. He is survived by his wife, 7-year-old son and 3-year-old daughter. PHILADELPHIA POLICE OFFICER KILLED, PARTNER SHOT 12 TIMES IN AMBUSH; SUSPECT FOUND HIDING IN TREE "He fought valiantly, but he lost his life today," Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel said at a news conference on Saturday. "His wife was able to be by his side before he passed, as well as his family." The wounded officer, a 33-year-old father of five, was shot 12 times and was initially listed in critical condition. He has since been listed in stable condition. The shooting unfolded around 12:20 a.m. Saturday, when the two officers responded to a report of a man with a gun. They located an armed man on a porch, according to police. KENTUCKY TROOPER, FATHER OF 3, GUNNED DOWN DURING TRAFFIC STOP AS SUSPECT CAPTURED AFTER MANHUNT The officers then came under "significant gunfire" after reaching the porch, police said. Additional officers and a SWAT team arrived a short time later and found both officers on the porch suffering from gunshot wounds. More gunfire followed, prompting authorities to declare a barricade situation before Lewis was eventually taken into custody, according to police. Police said Lewis was found in possession of two handguns and a shotgun. One of the handguns belonged to an officer wounded in the attack. At a news conference Saturday, District Attorney Larry Krasner declined to say whether Lewis had fired the officer's handgun or how he had obtained the other firearms. Krasner also said there was nothing in Lewis' criminal background that would have prevented him from obtaining a firearm. Lewis, an employee of the Philadelphia Water Department, has a criminal history dating to 2012, according to Pennsylvania court records reviewed by Fox News Digital. Court records show Lewis was convicted of theft and receiving stolen property in 2012 and of gun-related offenses and simple assault in 2013. He received probation in both cases. In 2018, Lewis pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct involving fighting and was again sentenced to probation. Fox News' James Cirrone, Brittany Miller and CB Cotton contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'Keep getting messages': Rahul Gandhi's big claim, and a message for CEC Gyanesh Kumar
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Monday levelled serious allegations against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Monday levelled serious allegations against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the Narendra Modi-led Centre, claiming that around 200 government officials were in touch with the opposition and sharing information, including officials from the Enforcement Directorate (ED), Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and the ministry of external affairs.Speaking at a press conference ahead of the INDIA bloc's planned march to the Supreme Court, Rahul said, "I want to tell Narendra Modi that 200 officials of your government are in touch with us and informing us, including those in the ED, CBI, foreign ministry..."Stepping up his attack on the poll body chief, Rahul claimed Kumar was having "sleepless nights" amid the opposition's campaign against alleged electoral irregularities.Responding to a reporter's question on whether he had communicated with the CEC, Rahul claimed that he had been "getting messages".When asked if he had a message for Gyanesh Kumar, Rahul said, "You have done a crime, and you are not the main criminal. You made a mistake and you are not the mind behind the mistake. We are after the people who are behind what you did. It is very easy for you, resign and get out of the way. We know that you have been forced by the Prime Minister, Amit Shah, Ajit Doval," Rahul Gandhi saidThe former Congress president also questioned why Kumar had not resigned, claiming that the opposition was receiving information from several sources."Why is all this happening? Because we are only asking the question raised by two Election Commissioners: why is Gyanesh Kumar not resigning? These days, we are receiving information from everywhere. Gyanesh Kumar, we know your situation. We know you are unable to sleep at night, and do not worry, we will not spare you. I am telling you directly that you will not escape as Election Commissioner because of what is happening."Rahul also accused the Centre of turning Delhi into a fortress to protect the CEC, as INDIA bloc leaders prepared to march towards the Supreme Court to demand Kumar's removal over alleged "vote chori" and concerns surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.He said a public movement against alleged electoral irregularities had been under way in Delhi for the past four to five days, with protesters demanding Kumar's removal."Since last 4-5 days, public movement is on in Delhi against 'vote chori', seeking CEC removal," the Raebareli MP said.Referring to the police action during the October 10 protests, Rahul alleged that authorities were preventing people from reaching the national capital by stopping trains and buses and forcing passengers to get off."People are being stopped from reaching Delhi. Trains and buses are being stopped, and people are being made to get off. Delhi has been turned into a fortress, with 20,000 to 30,000 police personnel deployed everywhere. Now, think about how powerful this is. But our strategy is different," the former Congress chief said.Questioning the security arrangements, Rahul accused the government of making a "grave mistake" by protecting Kumar. He argued that the heavy police deployment would only help the opposition draw attention to its allegations against the CEC and the Centre."We want 20,000 to 30,000 police personnel deployed on the streets. The government is committing a grave mistake, because we want to show the country that Modi ji wants to ensure the security of Gyanesh Kumar... The more he is protected, the more we will ultimately reach his controller... We are receiving reports that police personnel are distressed because they are being ordered to beat up young people, while instructions are being issued to give RSS members a free hand."Rahul further claimed that some police personnel supported the opposition's campaign and wanted it to continue."I am happy to tell you that 50% of the police personnel, and I am counting them, are telling us that what you are doing is right and that we should continue..."He also alleged that security personnel and ordinary citizens were increasingly opposed to the government's handling of the protests."Police, ITBP, CRPF, the people of India are on one side and Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Ajit Doval, Gyanesh Kumar, and 4-5 members of the Election Commission who are facilitating 'vote chori' and hijacking the country are on the other side. We are increasing this divide..."Rahul said the opposition's resistance had been building for years and was now taking a more concrete form."There was resistance from 12 years but it is getting crystallised now," he said.He also announced that INDIA bloc leaders would approach the Supreme Court on Monday with a petition against the CEC over alleged "vote chori".The press conference came ahead of the INDIA bloc's planned march to the Supreme Court, with opposition leaders seeking Kumar's removal amid mounting criticism of the SIR exercise.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Ukraine faces blackouts after Russian strikes despite 'energy ceasefire'
articles.summary: Power plants in Ukraine have been hit by Russia after Donald Trump's 'ceasefire' announcement.
articles.body:
Power plants in Ukraine have been hit by Russia, hours after Donald Trump said the two countries had agreed on an energy ceasefire.

Residents in the city of Izyum have been hit by blackouts after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, according to Ukrinform, Ukraine's state news agency.

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire "effective immediately", but gave no details. A ceasefire would see a pause on either country striking energy infrastructure targets.

Russia did not respond, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said such a deal would be "good news". He also accused Russia of striking Ukraine energy facilities after Trump's post.

What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?

Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants

Energy and railway infrastructure in the region of Zhytomyr in western Ukraine was also targeted by Russian attacks overnight, according to the head of the region's military administration, Vitaliy Bunechko.

On Sunday morning, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.

Ukrenergo did not say when the attacks occurred, but it said it would be introducing electricity rationing in parts of Ukraine "to avoid overloading the equipment damaged by previous Russian strikes".

After Trump announced the ceasefire on Sunday , Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect.

He wrote on social media: "Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this."

However, Zelensky said on Sunday evening that Russia had continued to launch strikes despite Trump's announcement.

He wrote on X: "There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.

However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."

Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".

For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure , disrupting energy supplies on both sides.

Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".

Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil a recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.

The deal, which would temporarily undo sanctions on Russian imports - is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in the US. It has faced criticism from Zelensky, European officials, and some US politicians.

articles.title: At least 72 Sudanese artisanal miners killed in strike, rights monitor says
articles.summary: At least 72 artisanal miners were killed in an airstrike in northern Sudan on Saturday, rights monitor Emergency Lawyers ‌said on Sunday, in the second such incident in several months.
articles.body: At least 72 artisanal miners were killed in an airstrike in northern Sudan on Saturday, rights monitor Emergency Lawyers ‌said on Sunday, in the second such incident in several months. Emergency Lawyers blamed the Egyptian air force for the strike, a claim Reuters could not immediately verify. The Egyptian military did not comment on the incident and Egypt’s foreign ⁠ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Images shared on social media and by local rights groups but not verified by Reuters show dozens of bodies strewn in rubble and others wrapped in funeral shrouds, and miners describing an airstrike on the area. Emergency Lawyers said such a cross-border attack would violate international law. Northern Sudan has seen an influx of artisanal miners and ‌makeshift ⁠gold mines as the country’s ongoing conflict disrupted other sources of livelihoods and gold became the key cash source for both warring parties. Experts and those in the sector say much of that gold is ⁠smuggled into Egypt. The war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has seen an increased frequency of mass-casualty events, particularly as drone ⁠warfare becomes the primary mode of fighting. On Friday, some 31 people were killed in a drone strike on a displacement ⁠camp in an army-controlled area of Sudan’s Blue Nile state, one of the war’s frontlines, according to the United Nations.

articles.title: Indian opposition defies lockdown, marches to demand election chief sacking
articles.summary: Opposition parties joined by student groups have petitioned the Supreme Court, seeking the election chief’s ouster.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India — India’s main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi led dozens of members of parliament and thousands of other protesters in a tense march to the Supreme Court on Monday, submitting a petition demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief even as tens of thousands of police officers shadowed them, stopping them from physically reaching the court.

Congress Party leader Gandhi was joined by his sister, Priyanka, who is also a member of parliament, and other prominent leaders on top of a truck that slowly made its way through a sea of supporters towards the court.

The police had set up a series of barricades to stop them from reaching the Supreme Court. But some Congress Party supporters crossed the first set of barricades after climbing over them. As they approached the second barricade, police officials tried to push back, and clashes appeared imminent.

But Congress leaders then announced that Gandhi and others had managed to submit their petition to the court, even if not physically, and their truck turned around.

Yet leaders from the Congress, other opposition parties and the Gen Z-led “Cockroach” protest movement have signalled that they are still deciding their next steps — their demand for Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation unchanged. The Cockroach Janta Party movement had forced out Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.

Rahul Gandhi, heir to India’s most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn a summer youth uprising into a broader challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s decade-long dominance of Indian politics, putting the Hindu nationalist government under growing pressure.

In a press briefing on Monday, Gandhi said the Modi government had put the capital city “in jail”. More than 30,000 police officers were deployed on New Delhi’s streets.

India’s Election Commission, a supposedly autonomous body tasked with overseeing the world’s largest electorate, has been criticised after revelations that its chief, Kumar, frequently overruled concerns raised by the other two election commissioners about the integrity of changes to the voter database.

For months, India’s opposition parties have argued that the election commission is compromised, sabotaging elections at the behest of Modi’s Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for its electoral benefit. The BJP denies the allegations.

Since June last year, the commission has been revising and updating statewide voter lists. It has since removed more than 130 million names, which critics say has disproportionately deprived minorities and other vulnerable groups in India of the right to vote.

Gandhi has called for the chief election commissioner to be tried for treason. “We will not spare you,” he said, referring to Kumar, at his Monday press briefing.

Opposition politicians allege that protest rallies by leaders including Gandhi have been met with violent and brutal force, as seen in videos showing them being detained.

“[The protesters] came with love in their hearts, not hatred or anger,” Gandhi said, referring to a protest on Saturday. “They were beaten, both by cops and BJP goons.”

“Narendra Modi … cannot silence India’s voice. These cowards cannot intimidate us. They will have to step aside,” he wrote on X, calling on people from all walks of life to join the protest on Monday.

Analysts say circumstances this time around are starkly different from the summer protests, when CJP-led demonstrators demanded the resignation of then-Education Minister Pradhan.

Asim Ali, a political analyst in New Delhi, told Al Jazeera that the mobilisation of the wider opposition would not stop, but the Modi government was unlikely to back down.

“The crackdown this time on students is making it apparent that it would be tougher for young protesters this time, and students can’t get beaten up and dragged violently daily,” he said. “Going forward, the opposition parties stand to be the front face of the protests, and they need to lead from the front.”

Since 1975, when then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a state of national emergency suspending civil liberties, “India saw more civil politics grow into mainstream, where opposition parties were allowed space,” Ali said.

He added that after five decades, “those democratic gains have vanished – and there are no constraints on this government by independent institutions.”

Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst, said he has seen New Delhi at the centre of “several big opposition political rallies, held in areas near the parliament, hosting hundreds of thousands of people”, when the police did not interfere, unlike the crackdowns this year.

Kidwai said that the violent detention of members of parliament, in particular, was worrying.

“We are seeing a big change from when politicians were more tolerant of dissent,” he noted.

With an unprecedented security deployment in central New Delhi designed to prevent protests, youth leaders are turning to new tactics.

Neha Bora, the president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a left-wing group affiliated with the Communist Party of India, has often tricked Delhi police in order to stage protests in recent days.

Bora, a post-doctoral student of theatre, came to national prominence for her fiery speeches in the July protests, becoming a leading face of the Gen Z movement challenging Modi’s Hindu nationalist politics.

Aditi Thakur, a 23-year-old student in the capital, has turned on notifications for all of Bora’s posts on social media. “A call to protest can come anytime, anywhere,” she told Al Jazeera.

Bora does not reveal when or where she is going to stage a protest until just 30 minutes before, to avoid detentions by the police. Her supporters are alerted via social media to join her at a given location in the capital.

On Sunday, she picked a congested street near central Delhi — and was able to jump several barricades to reach the heavily secured Parliament Street, before being chased down and dragged into a police van.

Even Thakur couldn’t catch her, she told Al Jazeera, laughing. “These are guerrilla times, but peacefully. If the government cracks down on us, we also need to adapt,” she said. “It is a fun cat-and-mouse chase every day. I’m hooked on it.”

The Gandhi-led Congress is also adopting similar measures, holding flash rallies at unannounced venues, then running away from police.

A defining feature of the July protests – a watershed moment for wrestling concessions from the government – was Gen Z’s humour in the face of police brutality.

Now, protesters are prepared for a more serious confrontation, even if demonstrations remain peaceful, say analysts.

“We are seeing that humour changing more into anger this time,” Asim Ali said.

The biggest challenge for the government is disruption in central New Delhi, which, Ali said, the government cannot allow on a daily basis. The area is home to most federal government offices, as well as being a major business hub.

Protesters know that too, and that gives them leverage.

“We are seeing this movement grow into a bigger anti-government, anti-Modi movement,” Ali said.

articles.title: Maps show how Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ keeps squeezing Palestinians in Gaza
articles.summary: A year into a ‘ceasefire’, Israel restricts access to 65 percent of Gaza and crams 2.1 million people into the rest.
articles.body:
Israel has expanded its military occupation in the Gaza Strip in violation of a United States-brokered ‘ceasefire’ , forcing Palestinians into an ever-smaller share of the besieged territory, devastated by Israel’s ongoing genocidal war.

Nearly two-thirds of Gaza is now under Israeli military control or subject to access restrictions.

The original ‘Yellow Line’, established under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end the war, marked the area to which Israeli forces initially withdrew. They were expected to make further withdrawals gradually, but instead, they have seized more territory.

On Sunday, Israeli forces moved yellow concrete blocks dozens of metres west in Shujayea, a neighbourhood in southeastern Gaza City, forcing Palestinian families to flee and bringing more of the neighbourhood under Israeli military control.

“It’s not simply about where the ‘Yellow Line’ is today but where it can move next,” Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili said, reporting from Gaza City. “For families who have been repeatedly displaced in the past three years, the situation remains dire, and they have to make the impossible decision of where they can go.”

More than 90 percent of Gaza’s 2.1 million population has been forcibly displaced by Israel’s war, launched on October 7, 2023, after Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

Using maps, Al Jazeera shows how much of Gaza Israel has grabbed since the ‘ceasefire’.

Before the war, Palestinians were spread across the Gaza Strip, a 365sq km (141sq-mile) territory roughly 41km (25 miles) long and from 6km to 12km (4 to 7 miles) wide.

That made it one of the most densely populated places on Earth with about 6,000 people per square kilometre, similar to Nairobi or London. Each person had, on average, about 160sq metres (1,722sq ft) of land.

Even then, not all of Gaza’s land was accessible. Israel enforced a buffer zone along the fence with Israel, and Palestinians who approached it risked being shot. In 2010, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimated that the restricted area covered 17 percent of Gaza’s land and 35 percent of its farmland.

Gaza has been under an Israeli land, air and sea blockade since 2007.

Under the first phase of the “ceasefire”, Israeli forces were to withdraw to the “Yellow Line” within 24 hours, after which a 72-hour period began for the handover of Israeli captives held in Gaza. Trump first published a map of the line on his Truth Social platform.

The line left Israel in control of 53 percent of the Strip, mostly farmland and border areas in the east, and confined Palestinians to the remaining 47 percent, about 172sq km (66sq miles).

By October 2025, two years of war had killed more than 67,000 Palestinians, and tens of thousands more had left the territory, reducing Gaza’s population to about 2.1 million.

Pushed into less than half of Gaza’s territory under the “ceasefire”, its density doubled to about 12,000 people per square kilometre, comparable to New York City. Each person was left with about 82sq metres (883sq ft).

Since the “ceasefire”, Israeli forces have repeatedly moved the yellow concrete blocks marking the “Yellow Line” farther west, sometimes overnight, expanding the areas under their control. Satellite imagery has also documented continued demolitions in areas held by Israeli forces.

The research group Forensic Architecture estimated that Israel controlled 58 percent of Gaza by December. In March, the Israeli military sent aid agencies maps of a new “orange line”, a restricted zone beyond the “Yellow Line” where humanitarian movements must be coordinated with the army.

According to OCHA, restrictions now cover 65 percent of Gaza. Israel itself said it controls about 70 percent of the territory, a UN official told the Security Council in June.

That leaves 2.1 million people in about 35 percent of the Strip, roughly 128sq km (49sq miles). The population density has nearly tripled since before the war to about 16,000 people per square kilometre, close to central Tokyo.

Each person now has about 61sq metres (657sq ft) of land for everything: shelter, roads, schools, hospitals and farmland.

Unlike Tokyo, Gaza has little space left to house its people. The UN Satellite Centre, UNOSAT, found 82 percent of structures in the Strip are damaged or destroyed. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization says only 3 percent of Gaza’s cropland is both undamaged and accessible.

OCHA says the remaining 35 percent of Gaza is “already overcrowded” and access restrictions are a key obstacle as aid groups try to relocate families before the rainy season. More than 950,000 people live in displacement sites at risk of flooding, according to the UN, most of them in tents and makeshift shelters, as seen in the satellite image below.

Approaching the ‘Yellow Line” can be deadly. Israel treats areas beyond it as a free-fire zone, and Palestinians who come near it have been shot. Nearly 1,500 people have been killed across Gaza since the ceasefire was announced.

articles.title: Melbourne man ‘strongly rejects’ links to flydubai attack suspect
articles.summary: Samir Mohtadi “strongly rejects” any attempt to associate him or Islamic centre in Melbourne with the alleged attacker.
articles.body:
A Melbourne man whose Islamic community centre has been linked by prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates to the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain of a flydubai jet has hit out at “false accusations”.

The Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda’s September 11, 2001 attacks, and carried out his attempt “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”, according to the Emirati prosecutor’s findings published by state media last week.

The prosecutor said the co-pilot, who has been identified in multiple media reports as Hamam al-Hammami, first became radicalised while studying in Australia “through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks”.

The prosecutor alleged he was acquainted there with an organisation known as “MyCentre” managed by a Lebanese man called Abu Hamza.

Neither “MyCentre” nor Abu Hamza are accused of any criminal wrongdoing.

In a video posted on social media on Sunday, Abu Hamza – also named by local media as Samir Mohtadi – rejected what he called “false accusations”.

“Right through the ages, those who’re righteous, they’ve always been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned — and this is the way it is”, he said in a four-minute video shared on MyCentre’s Facebook page.

He did not directly comment on the UAE prosecutor’s claims in the video, but in a separate statement cited by Australia’s ABC news outlet, Mohtadi was quoted as saying that he “strongly rejects” any attempt to associate him or the centre with the alleged attacker.

“The relevant authorities should have verified these claims with me before releasing or publishing such information,” the statement said.

“Throughout my life, I have consistently preached peace,” he said.

“Both in my work and the work of the centre have always focused on promoting peace, harmony, mutual respect and community wellbeing. We unequivocally reject violence in all its forms,” Mohtadi said.

“I strongly reject any attempt to associate me or [the] Multicultural Youth Centre with Al-Hammami. Such claims are unfounded, misleading and risk unfairly damaging the reputation of an organisation that has served the wider Australian community for decades.”

During the September 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help.

Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board “noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner”, according to the findings.

After gaining entry, he “intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect”.

Police and intelligence services in Australia and New Zealand are still investigating the alleged attacker’s links to both countries , where he allegedly spent time as a student and where he completed some of his flight training, according to national broadcaster Radio New Zealand (RNZ).
