articles.title: Why we love to dress for the job we don’t have
articles.summary: Today, most of us probably work from behind a desk. Yet our obsession with clothes from a different kind of working life just won’t quit.
articles.body: You’re a copywriter, a communications manager, an elusive creative director with indeterminate responsibilities. So why are you dressed liked a 20th century French rail worker? Today, some 70 million employed Americans will probably work from behind a desk. Yet our obsession with clothes from a different kind of working life just won’t quit. Between 1910 and 2000, blue-collar jobs such as mining, construction and manufacturing shrunk from 76% of the US workforce to 25%. Still, the workman image reverberates ad infinitum through the chore jackets, cargo pants and heavy-duty boots stocked in metropolitan shops, designer showrooms or spotted on the streets of fashion capitals like London, Paris and New York. The term “workwear” probably includes more clothing than you think, too. In his upcoming book, “Blue Collar Modernism,” menswear editor David Hellqvist gives a potted history of fashion’s biggest labels and their connection to occupation. Jeans, the bedrock of contemporary dressing, have their roots in the Californian mining industry of the 19th century. Even the small copper rivets that bookend our jean pockets, a feature so ubiquitous in modern denim it mostly goes unnoticed, were designed to reinforce the seams against ripping and keep the garment hard-wearing. The technology was patented as early as 1873. Elsewhere, Dr Martens were derived from a military boot, while Barbour’s well-to-do waxed jackets were first created as oil-skin outwear for fishermen and sailors in 1894. Utilitarian work clothes first left the factory floor in the early 20th century. Artists were an early group of adopters who helped recontextualize coveralls, jeans and chore coats, according to fashion historian Sonya Abrego. “Looking back, it can seem kind of edgy and cool and fashionable to us,” said Abrego, author of the 2022 book, “Westernwear: Postwar American Fashion and Culture,” in a phone call. “But they were really trying to make an anti-fashion statement.” Not to mention the fact these artists were still working people, completing a physical task that required some level of functional dress. Abrego points to a photograph of Jackson Pollock taken in his studio in 1949 for Life Magazine, kneeling on an enormous canvas dripping paint from a brush. “It’s all about the movement around the canvas,” she said. “And he’s got on jeans and a chore coat, it just goes together.” The Second World War helped globalize the working man’s garb further. Many of the American soldiers fighting overseas wore denim, often provided by Levi’s. The brand was recognized by the War Production Board and even had their costs set by the Office of Price Administration. When the war ended, Europe seemed besotted with this new, all-American textile — which had been catapulted into pop culture with films like “Streetcar Named Desire” (1952) and “Rebel Without a Cause” (1955). In fact, so enamored were the youth of Europe that in 1959 the New York Times reported a teenager in East Berlin was arrested for buying blue jeans in the city’s Western enclave. His sentence was two months, to “serve as a warning” to others hoping to try on this new democratic style for size. Almost 70 years later, workwear is one of fashion’s most enduring love stories. But why? These clothes are infused with a sense of nostalgia and reflect a quality of craftsmanship largely absent from affordable clothing today, thinks Abrego. “The connection to labor speaks pretty strongly,” too, she said. Maybe people are honouring a family history of trade, despite not working in these jobs themselves today. The draw is particularly strong for men’s fashion. “We’ve always looked to these kinds of professions for inspiration,” said Hellqvist. “Many of us aspire to be those kinds of men, who can fix things and do things. I know I certainly can’t, but I can pretend to be that guy.” With his book, Hellqvist set out to broaden the definition of workwear beyond the obvious legacy brands of Levi’s and Carhartt. “It’s not like miners in the gold rush anymore,” he said, “it’s office workers in the city.” Instead, Hellqvist covers the subculture’s history with a light touch and zooms out into a curated, highly shoppable list of labels he believes are pushing forward this style of dress in new ways. On his radar are Japanese brand Auralee (platformed by Lyst this summer as a rising star in data from the latest menswear shows); Fera, a British farmcore brand specializing in understated quilted vests and re-worked cotton Harrington jackets and Mfpen, a Copenhagen-based brand making relaxed tailored suits from deadstock fabric. Most of the designers included are, however, simply “inspired” by workwear, said Hellqvist. These next generation brands emulate the look of workaday garments without the purpose of a trade in mind or a “problem” to solve through clothing. But “the way they choose fabrics and the way they think about clothing in terms of functionality” keeps them in the lineage of predecessors like Dickies, Ben Davis and Vetra, he said. One contemporary brand keeping traditional job-driven design alive is Service Works, a London-based chefs-wear label founded by Tom Chudley in 2020. After more than a decade working in restaurants, Chudley told Hellqvist he became sick of the “plastic poly-cotton” that was “rubbing up and down my legs for 10 hours a day.” His clothing line makes traditional chefs pants in cotton canvas, aprons, chore coats rebranded as “Trade Jackets,” shirts, T-shirts as well as cotton double pleated trousers that can be worn by waiters and other catering staff. These garments are the defacto uniforms of London’s small plates scene, but they also have a fashion following from those outside the industry and are sold at retailers like End and Nordstrom. There is, of course, something ironic and even ahistorical about wearing blue collar clothes in a white collar world. There are those who balk at “people who pay a great deal of money to wear something that was worn by a sharecropper to sit at a desk all day,” said Abrego. Though personally, she doesn’t find it “that much more off-putting or hypocritical than anything else.” “I don’t really think there’s an authentic, real or true way to dress or present oneself,” she said. “If you want to wear cowboy boots and you don’t live in the West – go for it.”

articles.title: Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel in economics
articles.summary: American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics on Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
articles.body: American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics on Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the winners were being honored “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization.” “The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the academy said in a statement. Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone Monday from New York, saying: “It’s a tremendous honor, it’s a surprise.” “The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a news release. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.” The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust. The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896. Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’
articles.summary: The EU also announced that it officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military industrial complex.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” that United States President Donald Trump unilaterally announced at the weekend and promised to respond if the attacks continue.

Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum via video link on Monday, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to step in to ensure ⁠that Moscow abides by the truce in the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war , noting that there have already been “Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by ‌President Trump”.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “horribly surprised” that despite Trump’s announcement, Russia struck several energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv.

“We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, ⁠and we are waiting ⁠to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” he said.

“This ⁠energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending ‌the war if the Americans truly step in now and make ‌sure ‌Russians respect it … If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said talks for a possible “energy ceasefire” were ongoing, but rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal for a 60-day truce to allow elections to take place.

“In the Kremlin, both President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated we do not want a ceasefire,” Peskov said. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it.”

Trump’s announcement on Sunday that the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” caused confusion. It came two days after Trump declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage from European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Both Ukraine and Russia have been launching mutual attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure for months, adding to upward pressure on global energy prices that have risen amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

Zelenskyy initially denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him”, according to Axios.

Trump has previously taken to his Truth Social account to announce truces or other arrangements before either Kyiv or Moscow confirmed them.

“An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here in reality, not just on Truth Social,” Zelenskyy added.

European leaders expressed encouragement at the proposed ceasefire, but agreed with Zelenskyy that it had not taken effect.

“I have not noted, over‌ the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from the ‌Russian ‌side,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a Paris auto show.

At the Warsaw Security Forum, ⁠Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “Russia is not interested in ‌a ceasefire, de-escalation, or peace … that is why I will go to Brussels to urge all European partners ⁠to consider increasing ⁠sanctions.”

In Brussels, the European Union announced that it has officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military-industrial complex, including individuals and entities involved in the war, in a bid to maintain pressure on Moscow.

“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wrote online. “Europe is again showing a united front … We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians.”

Meanwhile, Russia ⁠attacked Ukrainian gas production facilities belonging to its state ⁠oil and gas ⁠company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, which caused a fire, the ‌company said on Monday.

“The attack damaged critical equipment. Our employees are doing everything possible ⁠to repair the ⁠damage as quickly as possible and ⁠prevent risks to ⁠the stable ⁠operation of the energy system,” Naftogaz acting CEO ‌Sergii Fedorenko wrote on Telegram.

A day earlier, Zelenskyy had said that Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Normandy veteran Henry Rice dies aged 100
articles.summary: Henry Rice, from Cranleigh, Surrey, was a signalman who served off Normandy in the days after D-Day.
articles.body:
World War Two veteran Henry Rice, who survived a near-miss when a torpedo was fired at the boat he was on, has died at the age of 100.

Rice, from Cranleigh in Surrey, was a signalman aboard HMS Eastway as part of the Normandy landings , arriving at Juno Beach five days after D-Day.

He received the Legion d'honneur from the French government and had called for schools to teach children more about the Normandy landings because the "world is dangerous at the moment".

A spokesperson from the Spirit of Normandy Trust, a charity for veterans, said: "Henry was a great character, with a cheeky smile that endeared him to everyone he met."

Rice previously told the BBC that revisiting Normandy for a remembrance service in June this year meant "everything" to him.

When thinking about veterans who had died, he added: "I find it too easy to wipe a tear away, so I don't let myself think too deeply. But when I'm on my own, then I do."

Troops from the UK, the US, Canada, and France attacked German forces on the coast of northern France on 6 June 1944, known as D-Day.

Rice delivered vehicles, men and equipment to reinforce the effort.

It was the largest military naval, air and land operation ever attempted and marked the start of the campaign to liberate Nazi-occupied north-west Europe.

Rice died just two weeks after Normandy veteran Kenneth Hay died at the age of 101.

Hay had survived being captured just weeks after D-Day and spent years educating children about World War Two.

The Royal Navy said Rice went on to Malta where he was land-based for 12 weeks before travelling through the Suez Canal into the Red Sea.

He spent some time based in the Gulf before going on to Sri Lanka, Burma and Singapore.

The Royal Navy said one of Rice's close encounters was a torpedo being fired towards the boat he was on, only for the missile to go beneath the hull.

In March this year, his family hosted a special celebration for his 100th birthday.

He told the BBC that, generally, veterans like himself only shared wartime experiences quietly amongst themselves.

"At home or with friends, you just say 'yeah, I was a matelot mate'," he chuckled.

The Spirit of Normandy Trust said he was committed to remembering those who were sent to war and never returned.

He attended remembrance events in the UK, including the Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey and the Cenotaph Parade.

At the planting of ceramic poppies at the Tower of London, he handed Queen Camilla the last poppy to be placed to mark VE Day 80 , according to the Spirit of Normandy.

Earlier this year, Rice met fellow D-Day veteran Ronald Hendrey, from Clacton-on-Sea in Essex for the first time to share memories of the Normandy invasion - one of his last acts of remembrance.

"He will be greatly missed by all and we offer his family our most sincere condolences," a Spirit of Normandy spokesperson said.

articles.body: Why some of Ken Paxton’s allies think he’s being sabotaged in the Texas Senate race. Errors by Flock license plate readers are leading police to pull over the wrong people. And Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers redeems himself in a win over the Colts. Here’s what to know today. Bad blood spills over in the Texas Senate race It’s been a brutal stretch for Republican Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton. Damaging leaks of his private conversations. Details of his past romantic affairs. Jabs at his physical appearance. And at least some of his allies are convinced the sabotage is coming from within his own party. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Wounds haven’t healed from the contentious primary in which Paxton defeated Sen. John Cornyn. Many in Paxton’s corner are convinced those aligned with Cornyn are trying to tank his chances. Others in the GOP say Paxton’s negatives are so high that few want to associate with him. Interviews with more than a dozen Texas Republicans involved in the crossfire make it clear there’s no hope for a truce before Election Day — or perhaps ever. Some say the fissures threaten to sideline GOP efforts ahead of a critical election. Read more about the bad blood. Meanwhile, Paxton’s Democratic rival James Talarico addressed his recent absence from the campaign trail yesterday, saying it was nothing but a “nasty case of the flu.” More election news: Analysis: Trump’s rallies are designed to pump enthusiasm into a base showing signs of fatigue and dissatisfaction. While the president can still bring a crowd like no one else in the Republican Party, he’s speaking in smaller venues — and often staring out at empty seats. Some say he may not be getting as much bang for his buck as he once did. Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews clashed over Iran, AI and Trump in their first debate. Abortion isn’t top of mind for voters, but Democrats are betting it could motivate their base. Across both parties, Black candidates look to make history in governor’s races. Flock ‘false flags’ lead to frightening motorist encounters with police Danny Brooks, an electrician in Indiana, was sitting in his company truck when police officers surrounded the vehicle, guns drawn. They handcuffed him and said the truck was reported stolen — but they had the wrong man. An error by a Flock license plate reader caused the mix up. These readers indiscriminately capture a photo of each car that passes its cameras. If one of the plates Flock photographs is on a “hotlist,” a law enforcement registry containing plate numbers suspected of connections to a crime, police are notified. But the system isn’t perfect. NBC News spoke with five people who have been pulled over or detained after Flock’s system raised false flags, including one who was jailed for nearly two weeks. We also analyzed logs showing officers searching and adding license plates to a system containing hotlists. Some officers intentionally added the wrong plate numbers to compensate for Flock mistakes. The Commanders had seconds left to secure a win — and blew it. They tied with the Giants 27-27 after Jayden Daniels’ poor decision to run the ball left the entire NFL in disbelief.In one of the craziest endings, the Eagles lost 19-17 to the Jaguars. Staff Pick: Frustrated by a slowing economy, young Chinese turn to Mao Zedong for guidance Fifty years after his death, China’s former leader Mao Zedong is finding renewed appeal among young Chinese people, who are flocking to his old residences and monuments to learn about his past and turning to his books for inspiration. They are drawing from his ideas to manage everyday challenges, from work and study to even video games. Some believe that the tightly controlled history textbooks and heavily censored internet in China might lead to an incomplete understanding of him, but this is not the only nor the primary reason behind the appeal. We travelled to Mao’s hometown of Shaoshan in southern China to speak with young visitors to find out how they felt seeing the site in person. We also spoke with two Chinese history experts to explore why Mao strikes a chord with a younger generation facing a slowing economy and growing social pressures. — Erin Tan and Dawn Liu, researchers based in Beijing Read All About It Kelly Clarkson says a Brooklyn store snubbed her. To counteract a spooky economy, America prepares to spend on Halloween candy. articles.title: Pennsylvania gunman who killed 8 was grandfather who seemed normal, victim relatives say
articles.summary: The Erie, Pennsylvania, gunman was a "good guy" before he "started going downhill," killing eight people and himself, a friend of a victim said.
articles.body: The man who killed eight, including a pregnant woman and two young children, in Erie, Pennsylvania, was a grandfather who did not appear distressed before the massacre, according to relatives of the victims. "I think that was a front for him," Julius Windham said Sunday while standing at a memorial for the victims, including his 1-year-old daughter, Amarianna, her pregnant mother, the woman’s 5-year-old son and her unborn baby. "Him every day, him smiling and being just — you would think of nothing like that would happen," Windham said. NINE PEOPLE KILLED IN PENNSYLVANIA SHOOTING; SUSPECTED GUNMAN FOUND DEAD: REPORT The 45-year-old gunman died of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after the Friday evening shooting, Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said. Authorities have not publicly identified the shooter or the victims, but Lorah said the gunman was related to seven of the eight people killed. The eighth victim was a friend of the pregnant woman. Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, said they had known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter "was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything." "They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?" Debra Eller said. "Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?" IOWA MAN SUSPECTED OF KILLING 6 FAMILY MEMBERS IN 'ACT OF EVIL' Mourners gathered Sunday outside the home where the shooting unfolded, leaving candles, flowers and stuffed animals. Windham wore a T-shirt showing photos of the women and children killed, along with the words, "Forever In My Heart." "Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now," Windham said. "But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody." Investigators recovered video and audio evidence that included muffled gunshots from inside the home shortly before two "distressed" women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came outside and shot the women as they ran toward him before returning inside. MONTANA MAN WHO KILLED 4 CHILDREN, 4 OTHER FAMILY MEMBERS AT SUNDAY DINNER WAS ASKED TO MOVE OUT: RELATIVE Officers arrived within minutes after receiving an alert through ShotSpotter, a gunshot-detection system, police said. No additional shots were fired after police arrived, Lorah said, adding that sounds later mistaken for gunfire came from flash-bang devices used by SWAT officers. Responding officers found the two women dead outside the home. After deploying a drone and robot, police entered and found the bodies of the 5-year-old boy and 1-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor. "Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home," Lorah said at a news conference. "But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole." 8 FAMILY MEMBERS, INCLUDING 6 CHILDREN, FOUND DEAD IN MICHIGAN FIRE; AT LEAST ONE VICTIM SHOT: POLICE Lorah declined to discuss a possible motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would interview relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home. "They knew something was going on at that house," Lorah said. "We have to figure out what that is." Lorah said the scene was devastating for first responders. "Some scenes stay with you long after you leave them. This is one of those tragic scenes," he said. DISPATCH AUDIO RELEASED IN MICHIGAN FAMILY MURDER-SUICIDE AS TROUBLED FAMILY'S SECRETS EMERGE Erie Mayor Daria Devlin said the police department "arrived at a horrific scene, faced unimaginable circumstances, and carried out their duties with courage and professionalism." "They too are members of this community, and they too will carry the weight of what happened last night," Devlin said at a Saturday news conference, addressing the victims’ families directly: "I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier. "Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you." Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he spoke with Devlin and offered his administration’s "full support" after what he called "the tragic mass shooting." Speaking later at a campaign rally outside Philadelphia, Shapiro also referenced the shooting of two Philadelphia police officers earlier Saturday. PHILADELPHIA POLICE OFFICER KILLED, PARTNER SHOT 12 TIMES IN AMBUSH; SUSPECT FOUND HIDING IN TREE "Today has been a dark day across this commonwealth," Shapiro said. District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public not to spread unverified information while investigators continue their work. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Please do not allow rumors, speculation or unverified information to add to the pain that these families are already experiencing," Hirz said. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Appeal for major energy storage system in Devon rejected
articles.summary: Plans for the battery system site near the Devon-Dorset border have again been dismissed.
articles.body:
Proposals to install a major battery energy storage system have been rejected after an appeal by the developer was dismissed.

Sky UK Development's plans for the battery system site (BESS) on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster were refused by East Devon District Council's planning committee last year.

The applicant appealed the decision with the Planning Inspectorate, proposing changes to mitigate concerns around groundwater contamination and the risk of battery units catching fire.

In her decision, inspector RC Kirby said such mitigation "would not be effective" in ensuring an acceptable balance between harm and benefit", stating the proposal was "not suitable for its location".

A key risk highlighted during the planning debate for the proposed BESS revolved around what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

Opponents claimed the amounts of water needed to contain such blazes and prevent their spread could mean any water running off into a nearby local waterway.

The appellant said it believed it would be about eight years before water used to fight a notional fire at the BESS would reach the drinking water source, but the inspector said there had been "insufficient evidence" to substantiate this.

The appeal decision notice stated the appellant had put forward revised plans that East Devon had not had put before it.

These included an increase in the size of the water tanks, relocation of some of the tanks, the separation distance between pairs of containers being 6m (20ft) apart, and other alterations.

Campaigners from Devon branch of the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) and the Hawkchurch and Monkton Wyld Action Group said they were "massively relieved" plans for the site had been blocked.

Devon CPRE energy spokesperson Dr Phil Bratby added: "For years, Devon CPRE has been highlighting the risks from the hazardous materials that could be released and contaminate the groundwater."

Kirby said that, while the benefits of the scheme would "outweigh the moderate harm that would be caused to the Dorset National Landscape", they were "insufficient" to outweigh the "very substantial, overriding, unacceptable risks in respect of pollution of the water environment".

Proponents of BESS systems highlighted their benefits in helping the nation reach net zero aspirations, notably because they could store energy.

The UK government noted BESS systems used batteries, for example lithium-ion batteries, to store electricity at times when supply was higher than demand.

"They can then later release electricity when it is needed. BESSs are therefore important for "the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable energy", it stated.

articles.title: Trump, Rubio consider firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece: AP source
articles.summary: President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of explosive reports alleging she engaged in misconduct during her tenure in Athens. A senior U.S. official told The Associated Press on Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely p‑‑‑‑d off” over Guilfoyle’s actions and…
articles.body:
President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of explosive reports alleging she engaged in misconduct during her tenure in Athens.

A senior U.S. official told The Associated Press on Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely p‑‑‑‑d off” over Guilfoyle’s actions and could decide on her future as soon as this week.

The official described the secretary of State, who received a warm welcome from Guilfoyle in Athens last week amid the reports, as particularly angry over the controversy.

A federal watchdog is also reportedly investigating her alleged misconduct, including additional accusations that the ambassador accepted gifts or favors from wealthy Greek businessmen.

The potential shake-up comes after longtime Trump ally and MAGA donor Eric Deters accused Guilfoyle of asking him to wire her $100,000 to pay her American Express bill ahead of her July 2025 Senate confirmation hearing in exchange for access to top Trump administration officials.

“It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” Guilfoyle wrote in a message on Signal to Deters on July 3, 2025, which was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

“She made it very clear, and the text messages make it very clear, she was so desperate for me to send that $100,000,” Deters said in an interview , claiming Guilfoyle offered to become his “ride or die in the Trump world” if he paid her and describing their relationship as a “quid pro quo.”

Trump briefly addressed the allegations, which Guilfoyle has denied, on Friday when questioned by reporters outside the White House.

“I just heard about it, too bad,” the president said. “I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice.”

Guilfoyle was once married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and was later engaged to the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., before the couple split in 2024.

Rubio refused to comment on the allegations while in Greece last week, telling reporters that it was not his responsibility to “respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what’s in there.”

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle allegedly boasted about her connections to wealthy Greek businessmen who paid for her luxury travel in exchange for using her diplomatic position to lobby on behalf of their business interests.

The diplomat also tried to secure an invitation from an American businessman in Davos, Switzerland, to a dinner honoring the president’s second-eldest son, Eric Trump.

“You know, I can deliver the world to you. Which you deserve,” Guilfoyle told an American businessman in the audio, reviewed by the Journal. “I’m going to make you a lot of f—ing money.”

In a statement to the outlet, a spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Athens defended Guilfoyle, saying she had “faithfully followed State Department ethics and gift reporting guidelines.”

The controversy was met with scrutiny from even top GOP lawmakers .

The Hill has reached out to the White House and the State Department for comment.

articles.title: Nobel economics prize awarded to Robert Hall and Michael ⁠Woodford
articles.summary: The Swedish academy says the academics’ models are ‘now used by central banks and governments around the world’.
articles.body:
The ⁠2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences has been awarded to US academics Robert Hall and Michael ⁠Woodford for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy, according to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

The winners of the prestigious award, formally known ⁠as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel and the final prize to be given out this year, were announced on Monday.

The two laureates developed new macroeconomic models that improve people’s ability to implement effective stabilisation policies, enabling fiscal and monetary policy measures that can reduce damaging swings in the economy.

“The laureates’ work has provided us ‌with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”

During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations stopped working. Hall and Woodford then developed new tools to understand what policy responses could be the most effective.

“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy said. “This encompasses an understanding of how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.”

The economics prize, first awarded ⁠in 1969, is not part of the five original awards ⁠created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was instead established by Sweden’s central bank.

The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ⁠ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for her work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time ⁠in the US.

Last year’s winners – Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt – won for ‌their work on “creative destruction” and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.

Like the other Nobel awards, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal, and a $1.2m cheque.

The Nobel prizes for medicine , physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last ‌week, with South African jurist Navi Pillay and Canadian writer Anne Carson among the winners.

articles.body:
Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) slammed President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia , a move that comes amid energy cost increases in the U.S.

“70% of Americans support Ukraine. Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” Bacon said Friday on the social platform X .

“The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity,” he added.

On Friday, Trump announced Russia will provide the U.S. and global market with diesel. The move comes only a few weeks out from the midterm elections, in which high energy prices are a central issue.

The president said Moscow will “immediately” give 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote Friday on Truth Social.

Trump’s deal comes amid fuel prices rising during the U.S. war against Iran, in which the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been closed.

According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. on Monday morning was about $6.27 per gallon, up from about $3.67 at the same time last year.

Bacon has a history of going after the White House over the Russia-Ukraine war, providing similar remarks in November of last year about being wary of Russia.

“I would like to see the president be a stronger advocate for the free country, the sovereign country of Ukraine that wants to be a democracy, wants to be allied with us, and have a little more clear-eyed view of who [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is, that Putin is the invader. He’s the dictator. He has murdered all of his opponents,” Bacon said in an interview on ABC News’s “This Week” at the time .

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Norfolk school stabbing trial hears from defendant's mum
articles.summary: The mother of a boy accused of attempted murder at a high school gives evidence at his trial.
articles.body:
The mother of a teenage boy who stabbed a girl in a masked attack at a school said she received a message from her son saying "sorry" shortly after the attack, a trial has heard.

Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March following reports a 15-year-old had been stabbed in the back.

The defendant, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, denies attempted murder, but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent.

After learning about the unfolding events on social media, his mother told the jury at King's Lynn Crown Court she "was in complete shock" when she realised her son was involved.

The mother told the trial that her son was "very quiet, very funny, very smart" and had a "dry sense of humour".

The court has previously heard how the defendant had written notes saying he hated women while the schoolgirl victim described to police how she told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed" .

During Monday's proceedings, the mother described the night before the attack as "completely normal", and said her son left for school at his usual time the following morning.

She said she first became aware something was happening when she was "doom-scrolling".

She messaged her son asking if he was OK, but said she did not "get an immediate response".

"When you realise there has been an incident at the school and you don't hear from children, it's worrying," she said.

She had the ability to see her son's location using a phone app, and messages on social media had said there had been a knife attack and that someone had left the school grounds.

"When I saw he wasn't at school and someone had run away I was concerned [my son] was involved," she told the court.

She said she received a message on her phone saying "I'm sorry", and when she called her son and asked what had happened, he replied "nothing good" and that he had "hurt someone".

She told the court her son did not sound like himself, spoke in "very short sentences" and "sounded very upset".

Alongside her husband, she went to try to find her son and was passed by two police cars "with blues and twos on".

She called 999, gave the police her son's location, and was advised to head home.

"I was in complete shock," she told the court.

Prosecuting counsel Christopher Paxton, KC, asked the mother if there were any concerns about how her son was using his phone and if she was checking his phone.

A teacher who chased the boy following the attack described how the then 15-year-old had "legged it".

He told the court that a person who witnessed the stabbing came to him and said "she's been stabbed".

When he went to the corridor, the teacher said "the only person I saw was dressed completely in black".

He said he was "very shocked" and shouted to the boy to stop.

He told jurors he ran after the boy for about 25 seconds and continued to shout "stop" and saw that a black glove had been dropped.

articles.title: A 17-member $900,000 expedition set out on an 830-nautical-mile voyage to Nikumaroro to inspect a submerged object seen in satellite images; five days of sonar, magnetometer and dredging could test an Amelia Earhart theory
articles.summary: A 17-member team backed by Purdue University embarks on an expedition to Nikumaroro to investigate a submerged object that may be related to Amelia Earhart's disappearance in 1937. The mission includes advanced sonar, magnetometry, and dredging techniques to uncover the truth behind one of aviation history's greatest mysteries.
articles.body: A team of marine archaeologists is heading to a remote Pacific island to investigate an object that could provide new clues to the disappearance of aviator Amelia Earhart in 1937. Backed by Purdue University, the team will examine an object in a lagoon at Nikumaroro to determine whether it could be part of the Lockheed Electra aircraft Earhart was flying when she vanished.Amelia Earhart was an American aviator who became the first woman to fly solo and nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean in 1932. She disappeared in July 1937 while attempting to fly around the world with her navigator, Fred Noonan. Their aircraft vanished over the Pacific, leaving one of aviation history’s most enduring mysteries.According to Purdue University, the object, known as the Taraia Object, was first spotted in satellite images in 2020 and is also visible in aerial photographs dating back to 1938. The expedition team believes its shape resembles an aircraft's body and wings, although the theory remains disputed.Team to examine the objectThe 17-member expedition is being led by Richard Pettigrew of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, working with Purdue University and the Purdue Research Foundation. The team is travelling aboard the Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel Marin Mainiku to Nikumaroro, an uninhabited island in Kiribati's Phoenix Islands.The researchers plan to spend five days on the island before returning to Tarawa, Kiribati’s capital. They will first use a drone to survey the area and then deploy specialized equipment to examine the object beneath the surface.The team plans to use sonar, which helps detect objects underwater, and magnetometers, which measure magnetic fields and can help identify metal objects. After these surveys, the researchers intend to use a hydraulic dredge to uncover the object.“Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” Pettigrew said in materials released for the expedition.Steve Schultz, Purdue's senior vice president and general counsel, is leading the university's expedition team. Speaking to Reuters, he said finding the aircraft could resolve a longstanding aviation mystery.“This would be solving one of the great mysteries in aviation history, certainly one of the great mysteries of the 20th century,” Schultz said.The mission has a budget of $900,000. Purdue has a historical connection to Earhart, who worked at the university as a career counsellor for women and an adviser to its aeronautics department. A university research grant also helped fund the development of her Lockheed Electra aircraft, which she called her “flying laboratory”.Why the island mattersNikumaroro has long been at the centre of one theory about Earhart’s disappearance. Some researchers believe she and Noonan may have reached the island after failing to find Howland Island, where they had planned to refuel.According to this theory, the pair landed on or near Nikumaroro and died there. Supporters point to objects found on the island, including a glass jar from the 1930s used for freckle cream and parts of a pocketknife similar to one Earhart reportedly carried.Researchers have also examined measurements of human skeletal remains found on the island in the 1940s, radio signals recorded after the aircraft disappeared and a photograph of the island’s shoreline taken months later.Ric Gillespie, co-founder of The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery (TIGHAR), has investigated the island through 12 expeditions over three decades. He has argued that an object visible in the shoreline photograph resembles the aircraft's landing gear.However, the evidence has not established that Earhart reached Nikumaroro. Gillespie told Reuters that two earlier searches for the aircraft in nearby waters, including a 2019 expedition led by marine archaeologist Robert Ballard, failed to locate the wreckage.The US government's longstanding position, as reported by Reuters, is that Earhart's aircraft ran out of fuel and crashed into the sea near Howland Island, about 400 miles northwest of Nikumaroro.Researcher says the object could be a treeGillespie supports the broader possibility that Earhart reached the island but doubts the latest team will find the plane.He believes the object in the lagoon is actually a fallen pandanus tree, a palm-like plant native to the region. He says the images show the tree’s roots and branches.“You can see the root ball. You can see the branches,” Gillespie said. “It's a tree. People see what they want to see.”Gillespie believes that even if Earhart’s plane landed on the island, it may later have been swept into the sea by tides and broken apart by waves.“I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen,” he said.The expedition team disagrees that the object can be dismissed without further investigation. It believes the shape seen in the images is worth examining more closely.What happens if the team finds the plane?The expedition will first try to establish what the object is. Schultz said the team would not remove any parts from the aircraft during this trip, even if the researchers identify it as Earhart’s plane.Any attempt to recover wreckage would require further permission from the Kiribati government.You use AI every day. articles.body: Saudi Arabia on Monday said it plans to increase its crude oil export capacity through pipelines up to 10 million barrels per day by converting a domestic gas pipeline for oil shipments and upgrading its existing East-West network.Energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said the kingdom could add up to 1.2 million barrels per day of export capacity within seven to eight weeks by temporarily repurposing a gas pipeline to transport crude oil.Further investments could increase the additional capacity to as much as 3 million barrels per day, Abdulaziz said at the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh.The minister said he had authorised Saudi Aramco to use the pipeline for oil transport until May. It would then need to be cleaned and restored to gas service ahead of the summer season.Upgrades to pumping stations along the East-West pipeline, along with other infrastructure projects, could help Saudi Arabia raise its capacity to redirect shipments from its main maritime routes in the Gulf and Red Sea to around 10 million barrels per day over the next two to three years, Abdulaziz said.Meanwhile, Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said the company was examining additional routes for crude oil exports and working to expand its overseas storage capacity.Oil exports from the Middle East have largely recovered to pre-war levels as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has increased, Reuters reported.Data from Kpler showed that total crude oil and condensate exports from the region, excluding Iran, averaged 18.11 million tonnes a week in September. articles.title: Coast-to-coast cleanup after three storms batter North America
articles.summary: North Americans are dealing with the aftermath of three storms that battered the continent’s coasts this weekend.
articles.body: North Americans are dealing with the aftermath of three storms that battered the continent’s coasts this weekend. Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 storm. It forced evacuations along the Florida Panhandle and in some areas of Alabama. At least four people were killed in the storm, including Jennifer Williams, whose family said she died when a tree fell into her home. Her husband, Joey, told NBC News that a tree hit their Pensacola home, crushing their family room and killing her instantly. At least one other person was killed due to a downed tree in Alabama. Another died of carbon monoxide poisoning from a generator running in his garage in Florida, and a fourth person was killed in a motor vehicle crash in Alabama, The Associated Press reported. Video from the storm showed intense winds tearing the roof off a hotel in Pensacola. It also sent a massive tree through a man’s house and into his bedroom. The man, Darryl Wellens, and his wife barely survived — he said they were inside the house when the tree fell. Crews are working to restore power for hundreds of thousands in Florida and Alabama. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said power should be restored at some point Monday. DeSantis has also warned of potential river flooding in the coming days. Many people in Isaias’ path remain under boil-water advisories. Isaias continued north Sunday, dumping heavy rain across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic. North Carolina saw major flooding and landslides, while the rest of the area faced a deluge all day. At least 22 tornadoes were reported on the East Coast as Isaias inched north. The storm also wreaked havoc on long-weekend travel plans. The remnants of the storm are exiting the New England coast Monday morning and moving out to sea, and most of the rain is going with them. They will continue to move east Monday, paving the way for a nicer Tuesday. Hurricane Simon hits Mexico without making landfall — yet Hurricane Simon, a Category 3 storm, pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast Sunday, but its eye remained offshore, keeping it strong. The heaviest rains and winds battered the Puerto Vallarta area Sunday with maximum sustained winds of 120 mph. Some areas saw up to 8 inches of rain. Simon is moving parallel to the country’s western coast Monday and is expected to make landfall and then dissipate inland over Mexico. Winds had dropped to 115 mph by early Monday, as the storm crawls northwest at 5 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center. Hurricane warnings are in effect for Playa Perula to El Roblito and Las Islas Marias. A hurricane watch is in place north of El Roblito to Bahia Tempehuaya. Tropical moisture from the storm is expected to stream into the U.S. and bring the risk of flooding to the middle of the country later this week. The same region could see 1 to 3 inches of rain Wednesday and Thursday, with up to 6 inches in some areas. Remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel continue to dump rain on the Southwest Meanwhile, people on the West Coast are facing flooding after Tropical Storm Rachel barreled through over the weekend. Videos showed Las Vegas under feet of water, and huge waves were seen battering homes along beaches in Southern California. Las Vegas saw more than an inch of rain, breaking the daily record for Oct. 11, which was set in 2012. The remnants of Rachel continued to bring rain and some flooding to parts of the Southwest on Monday, even reaching as far north as southeastern Idaho. Flash flood watches and warnings are in place for most of the region, including in Arizona, Nevada, Utah and Idaho. In some areas, up to 3 inches of rain is possible Monday. A coastal flood advisory is in effect for Southern California, where high tides and surf could cause problems. More tropical downpours are likely Monday for the Southwest, Four Corners and central Rockies. Some snow is also possible in higher-elevation areas.

articles.title: Álvaro Pulido: US detains man accused in multi-billion Venezuelan money laundering scheme
articles.summary: US officials had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to Álvaro Pulido's arrest.
articles.body:
A Colombian man wanted for allegedly laundering money that had been illegally syphoned off a Venezuelan government welfare plan has been detained in the United States.

The US Department of Justice said Álvaro Pulido, 62, had been arrested during a Homeland Security Task Force operation on Sunday, but did not provide further details as to how he ended up in US custody.

Pulido had been in jail in Venezuela since March 2023 accused of diverting profits from the state-run oil company PDVSA.

The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and State Department had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to his arrest.

He is due to appear in court on Tuesday, according to a statement released by the US Attorney's Office.

Pulido's arrest comes just two months after Alex Saab, another Colombian businessman with close ties to the Venezuelan government, pleaded guilty to money laundering charges in a US court.

The US State Attorney's Office said that Pulido had been charged in two separate federal indictments "involving the alleged laundering of more than $2bn (£1.5bn) in connection with Venezuelan government bribery schemes".

US prosecutors say Pulido, along with four other co-defendants, bribed Venezuelan government officials to secure contracts to provide poor Venezuelans with food and medicine.

They accuse Pulido of wildly overcharging the Venezuelan government and laundering the profits through bank accounts abroad, including in the US.

They also allege that Pulido worked with Alex Saab to launder $350m from a separate bribery scheme involving Venezuela's currency exchange system using bank accounts in Florida.

Until recently, Saab was a powerful figure in the Venezuelan government with close ties to the then-leader, Nicolás Maduro, who named him minister of industry in 2024.

However, after Maduro was seized by US forces in a raid on Caracas in January and taken to New York to stand trial on drug-trafficking charges, Saab's fate quickly changed.

Less than two weeks after Maduro was seized, the new US-backed interim government of Venezuela sacked Saab from his post as minister, and in May it extradited him to the US.

Last month, Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.

articles.title: Russia targets Ukraine energy facilities despite Trump’s energy ceasefire claim
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday that Russia has continued to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, violating what Trump claimed was an energy ceasefire agreed to between the two countries. Zelensky said Russian forces struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv and other energy facilities, despite Trump’s declaration on Sunday that both countries had agreed to…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday that Russia has continued to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, violating what Trump claimed was an energy ceasefire agreed to between the two countries.

Zelensky said Russian forces struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv and other energy facilities, despite Trump’s declaration on Sunday that both countries had agreed to immediately stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure.

“It is clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social, and his ‘shahed’ drones follow a different set of instructions,” Zelensky wrote Monday on the social platform X .

Trump announced the ceasefire Sunday on Truth Social following a phone conversation with Putin, stating that both sides had agreed to the ceasefire and warning them not to violate it.

Zelensky was caught off guard by the announcement, and he said at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland that Ukraine had learned of the deal through news reports.

He said Ukraine supported the proposal but made it clear that Kyiv would not agree to stop its retaliatory strikes without a corresponding halt to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy system.

“If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure. This is only fair,” Zelensky wrote.

Zelensky urged the Trump administration to secure Moscow’s compliance, saying the agreement could help pave the way toward ending the more than four-year war.

Tensions escalated between Trump and Zelensky over Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, which the president has blamed for causing U.S. diesel prices to surge ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Trump warned Zelensky on Saturday that he had “better damn well stop” attacking Russian refineries, a day after reaching an agreement with Putin to purchase 300,000 tons of Russian diesel in an effort to lower fuel prices.

Zelensky blasted the diesel deal , arguing the move will provide the necessary funding to further fund Russia’s war in Ukraine.

“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” Zelensky wrote in a lengthy post on X . “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”

articles.title: Why are the Houthis striking Saudi airports?
articles.summary: The attacks mark the deadliest assault on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack that killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh – the day after another attack killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

The attacks mark one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years and the deadliest assault on Saudi soil in more than a decade, as Yemeni government forces are also targeting airfields in Houthi-controlled territory.

The sharp escalation in the war’s new front comes amid fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, following the collapse of a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely in place since 2022.

Which Saudi airports have the Houthis hit?

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh: The airport in the Saudi capital has been struck four times in the past five days. Saudi authorities reported that one person was killed and eight wounded on October 7 . The following day, a raid killed an airline pilot and two other Saudi citizens, with several others wounded.

King Fahd International Airport in Dammam: Houthis claimed an attack on the airport in Dammam, the industrial port city on the Gulf coast, on Sunday.

Abha International Airport: On October 7 , two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at the airport, the civil aviation authority said.

King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan: On October 6 , Saudi authorities reported attacks on the southern airport that injured three people.

Najran Airport: The same day, Saudi authorities said Najran Airport was hit and reported minor injuries.

Have Yemeni forces hit Houthi-held airports too?

Yes. Houthi-run media on Sunday reported “Saudi” air strikes targeting areas in Yemen’s capital Sanaa, held by the Iran-backed armed group.

The reports said the attacks targeted the Airport Road area of Sanaa’s al-Thawra district, as well as the Hamdan district. There was no information on the results of those attacks.

Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia also hit Sanaa airport on July 13 with at least five munitions in a series of air attacks, three of which directly struck the only working runway.

The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014. Battles are raging around the southern cities of Mocha and Dhubab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

The vital shipping chokepoint has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz , where Iranian attacks have raised the costs and risks for oil tanker operators.

Why are Houthis attacking Saudi airports?

The attacks have emptied skies over the Saudi capital Riyadh, as ‌‌‌‌authorities extended the suspension of operations at the city’s international airport, the second-busiest after Jeddah.

Lufthansa has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16 , while Air France-KLM extended its previous ⁠⁠⁠⁠suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month. The UK, France and Germany have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh.

The disruption comes as the country hosts two major Saudi energy and investment conferences.

Organisers of the World ⁠⁠⁠⁠Petroleum Congress (WPC), set to host top global oil executives and policymakers from Sunday to Thursday, said it was proceeding as planned. The Future Investment Initiative, launched by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as the kingdom’s flagship investment conference a ‌‌‌‌decade ⁠⁠⁠⁠ago, would also proceed as planned from October 26-29 .

Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told the WPC that the kingdom’s resilience had been put to the test, but sought to reassure attendees at the high-profile conference that its response would be “equally serious”.

The kingdom, which is preparing to host the 2032 FIFA World Cup, has long sought to market itself as a secure destination for major events, global tourism and investments.

Hisham al-Omeisy, a conflict analyst and adviser at the European Institute of Peace, predicted that the Houthis would escalate attacks to include oil pipelines and energy facilities – and continue attacks on airports because of the strong “public response” to hitting such targets.

“Houthis have escalated massively, they’ve crossed that line… they have their own frameworks, their own calculations and stopping at attacking a civilian airport is not one of those calculations,” al-Omeisy told Al Jazeera.

“They are a maximalist group and they’re there to do whatever they need to do to get to what they want,” the analyst said, including “more concessions from the Saudis.”

Why are Yemeni forces attacking Houthi-held airports?

The Yemeni capital hosts the only airport providing international flights to and from Houthi-controlled territory, where the majority of Yemen’s population lives.

The Houthi-run broadcaster also reported attacks on Thursday on Hodeidah International Airport on the Red Sea coast, without specifying the extent of the damage.

Yemeni representatives at the UN have claimed that those airports are being used to shuttle Houthi delegations to and from Iran, which backs the group. According to the government of Yemen, the attacks have hit airport facilities to prevent Iranian flights from landing there.

articles.title: Murder-accused and teen had 'beef' before fatal stabbing - court
articles.summary: Tristan Kerr, 17, bled to death minutes after being stabbed in the heart and lung, a court heard.
articles.body:
A man accused of murdering a teenager along with three others had been involved in a disagreement with him in the weeks before he was stabbed to death, a court has heard.

Tristan Kerr, 17, from Abertridwr, in Caerphilly, bled to death in the street minutes after being stabbed in the heart and lung with a so-called Zombie knife on 5 February.

Connor Palfrey, 25 from Abertridwr, Georgie Mears, 19, from Thornhill, Cardiff, Elexi Manny, 25 from Senghenydd, Caerphilly, and Ricardo Elliot, 27 of no fixed address, all deny murder through joint enterprise.

Joint enterprise means people who assist or encourage another person to commit a murder can be convicted for the same crime.

Kerr was attacked in the living room of the flat in Lower Francis Street in Abertridwr which was home to Ieuan Crane, 31, the court heard.

Giving evidence from a video-linked room at Newport Crown Court, Crane said Palfrey had what he described as "beef" with Kerr following an incident in which the teenager was said to have chased Palfrey with his dog.

"He [Kerr] was just chasing him," Crane said.

"At that time there was a beef. A week or two after he went to see Connor Palfrey and they squashed their beef," he said, meaning they resolved the issue.

On the day the teenager died, Crane said he, Kerr and two other men were sitting in the living room of his flat "just chilling" and playing computer games and watching YouTube when Palfrey and Mears burst in through the unlocked front door.

In a police video interview played to the jury Crane said Palfrey had been armed with a block of wood that "might" have had a nail in it.

He said Mears ran ahead of Palfrey and began attacking Kerr, who had been sitting on a two-seater sofa close to the stairs.

He told officers that at first, he did not realise Mears was armed with what he later described as a "big" knife with a "Zombie, Rambo blade".

"I didn't see the knife until after the fourth time," he said.

Crane said he tried to grab Mears' arm and wrist, but Palfrey threatened him with the block of wood. He said he was trying to stop the attack on his friend.

Kerr and another friend known as "Custard" escaped through the back door of the flat.

Crane said he threw Palfrey and Mears out of his home, and that Manny and Elliot had been in the hallway.

"I pushed them out of the house and locked the door, they went in the car, the car was on the drive," he said.

Crane said he only realised Kerr had been badly hurt when he went out into the street and his friend Custard told him: "It's bad."

"I didn't even know if he was hurt or nothing. I didn't see no blood as he ran out. I thought he was sound, then I saw him collapsed in the street.

"I could see blood dripping down to his socks, he had white socks. I didn't know what to do. I couldn't move him.

"A lady came out, a nurse, looking for a stab wound trying to clean it."

Crane said he had known Kerr for two years, and that the teenager came to his flat every day to see his lurcher greyhound cross dog which Crane was looking after.

He said Kerr would come to visit in the morning or afternoon but had to leave by 20:00 because he was on an electronic tag.

A large quantity of cannabis was later found in the freezer at the Lower Francis Street flat along with a shotgun cartridge and weighing scales.

In cross examination, Crane admitted smoking cannabis, but said he had forgotten about the drugs in the freezer and did not know anything about the weighing scales or the shotgun cartridge.

He said he did not "knowingly" allow any of his friends to deal drugs from his home.

Asked by Chris Rees KC, defending Mears, if Kerr dealt drugs, Crane said he was "not sure".

"Tristan Kerr was dealing drugs from your address?" Mr Rees KC asked. "Not to my knowledge," Crane replied.

He said he knew the teenager was taking ketamine.

The four defendants were later arrested in Hereford.

articles.title: Trump ‘thinking of’ renaming Atlantic or Pacific
articles.summary: President Trump over the weekend said he was “thinking of” renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, a move that comes after the president’s previous moves to rebrand geographical features. articles.body:
President Trump over the weekend said he was “thinking of” renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, a move that comes after the president’s previous moves to rebrand geographical features.

During a rally in Tennessee on Saturday, the president discussed his renaming efforts for Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico.

“So, we need a river, we need an ocean. So, I was thinking of either the Atlantic or the Pacific,” Trump told the crowd at the rally. “We call it ‘Trump Ocean’ or ‘Ocean of the America,’ something like that.”

In late August, Trump signed an executive order formally changing the name of Lake Ontario, which shares a name with the Canadian province, to “Lake America” amid trade tensions with Canada.

“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters at the time.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed back on the lake renaming , explaining the history of Lake Ontario’s Indigenous name on social media.

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” Carney wrote on the social platform X at the time.

Last year, Trump also signed another executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

articles.summary: Experts weigh in on vibration plates and whether they can help you workout and lose weight.
articles.body: The latest viral fitness trend is literally buzzy. Vibration plates are all over TikTok, with devotees saying they help tone and strengthen muscles. Never heard of them? “A vibration plate, also known as a power plate, is a machine that vibrates when you stand on it,” says John Gallucci Jr., a doctor of physical therapy and CEO of JAG Physical Therapy. “This forces your muscles to constantly contract and relax.” Unlike sneakers, stationary bikes or ankle weights, vibration plates seem a bit more complicated to use. And do they even work? To answer these questions and more, I spoke with physical therapists — here’s what they had to say. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Do vibration plates work? With so many ridiculous wellness fads out there, I was skeptical when I first started seeing videos of people standing on these vibrating devices pop up in my feed. So, the first question I asked the experts I spoke with was whether they actually have any benefits. The answer: They may. There is some truth to their effectiveness — but research behind them is mixed, so it those benefits may not be quite as strong as the hype suggests, says Thomas R. Denninger, a physical therapist at ATI Physical Therapy. So what do vibration plates actually do? “They cause your muscles to quickly tighten and relax over and over, as they are working to keep your balance,” says Denninger. “Because your body has to work a little harder to stay steady, you may feel like your whole body is working.” Here are some of the potential benefits, according to Denninger: They can help your muscles turn on and work harder, especially during simple exercises like squats or bridges.Because the surface is shaking, your body has to constantly adjust. Over time, this can help with balance and body awareness.You may feel less stiff after using them because the vibration temporarily increases blood flow. While all of these benefits are possible with regular use, Denninger stresses that a vibration plate should not replace regular exercise. “Think of it more as a workout booster, not a cure-all,” he says. Highly-rated vibration plates The list below includes vibration plates recommended by experts. I also included highly rated options with at least a 4-star average rating from over 500 reviews at popular retailers. Gallucci likes this vibration plate because it’s compact, lightweight and has a lot of power and speed settings. It also comes with a remote and resistance bands that you can use while on the plate. The top of the plate is covered with an anti-slip material to keep you secure and it has a hidden handle and wheels to make transporting it easy. Ideal for those who don’t have much space, this vibration plate is just over 12 inches wide and nearly 18-inches long. It also weighs under 20 pounds and is the lightest option on this list. It has an anti-slip coating on it and a large LED screen so you can see your settings. It also comes with a remote and resistance bands you can use while on the plate. If you’re willing to splurge, consider this linear vibration plate. It is simple to use and lightweight, according to Gallucci, who says it is a good option for beginners. The machine has three programs — cardio, detox and muscle — and it has a timer that you can set for anywhere between one and 20 minutes. It also comes with a remote. This vibration plate can hold up to 400 pounds and is nearly two feet wide to accommodate larger bodies. It also has Bluetooth connectivity, so you can pair it with your phone and stream music while you work out. Many reviewers also note that it is very quiet and helps with recovery after a workout. If you struggle with balance, consider this vibration plate with a handlebar. Don’t need it? You can lower it and use the included resistance bands to amp up your workout. Reviewers also say that it feels very stable. Along with a non-slip coating, the underside has suction feet to help it stick to the ground. How to shop for a vibration plate If you are interested in adding a vibration plate to your workout routine, experts I spoke with recommend keeping the following in mind as you shop: Type: There are three different types of vibrations. Oscillating plates have a side-by-side motion, linear plates move up and down and combination plates do both. “Each type of plate works different muscle groups,” says Gallucci. A combination plate will cover more bases, so I focused on those for this list.Size: Before you purchase a vibration plate, think about where you are putting it. You’ll want to make sure it fits comfortably in your intended space and that it will hold your weight comfortably, says Gallucci. Most vibration plates should indicate the maximum weight they can hold.Settings: “Speed settings are important,” says Gallucci. “A vibration plate with multiple speed options allows users to tailor the intensity of their workouts according to their fitness levels and goals.” Meet our physical therapy experts​​ At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience.
